articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

ARTEX is a Chinese open-source, AI-powered penetration testing platform designed to help security teams assess systems they own or are authorized to test. In recent weeks, it has been used in traditional cybercrime campaigns, including in attacks on South Korean banks. Although the original developer made ARTEX closed-source in mid-October, actively maintained forks and backups of the original repository remain publicly available to threat actors.

Nation-state actors swiftly adopted this new tool: a China-nexus espionage actor used ARTEX against more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries. Another China-state aligned actor, who was responsible for the October 2026 ConnectWise supply chain compromise, used ARTEX to attempt mass sign-ins to more than 2,250 Azure tenants.

We assess with high confidence that ARTEX marks a change in the threat landscape: agentic offensive frameworks have moved from experiments to operational use by state-aligned and financially motivated actors alike. Since late August 2026, at least five actors and clusters have used ARTEX, from China-nexus espionage groups to a Cambodia-based criminal cluster. Closing the source in early October did not slow adoption.

The barrier to entry is low: Operators ran ARTEX in default configurations, and each campaign cost $145 to $1,500 in model time. The agents work at machine speed: in one case of suspected ARTEX use, an agent went from a leaked GitHub secret to Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. They can also be told to look for gaps, e.g. a Chinese-aligned actor told its agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor.

We expect more actors to adopt ARTEX and similar frameworks such as PentAGI and Cairn. For defenders, the time between a leaked secret or an exposed flaw and its exploitation can now be minutes, and IP blocklists lose value against agents that rotate through residential proxies. Rotating secrets, closing internet-facing flaws, and EDR coverage on every host now matter more than simply blocking indicators.

Key Highlights

A tool built for authorized testing now runs criminal campaigns. Across the 10 instances Check Point analyzed, operators used ARTEX exclusively for opportunistic, financially motivated cybercrime, mostly on a broad scale. The operators ran default configurations with default tools.

State-linked actors use it, too. For instance, a China-nexus espionage actor, used ARTEX against more than 200 organizations from October 17, 2026. Its operator told the agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor.

A supply chain compromise fed ARTEX more than 2,250 targets. Storm-0940 gained control of the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications, including Cloud Backup, and used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants.

The agents ran without an operator. In multiple campaigns, nobody prompted the agents after the operator set the initial task goals.

The campaigns were cheap and the losses were real. Observed campaigns cost an estimated $700 to $1,500, recovering more than 300 signing certificates with their passwords or more than 190,000 Honor of Kings credentials, about 6,000 of them still valid, in exchange.

From GitHub to Key Vault in 5 minutes. In at least one case of suspected ARTEX use, an AI agent moved from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

What Is ARTEX

ARTEX is an agentic AI penetration testing platform that, by default, uses off-the-shelf tools like Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium, among others. Many operators routed their agents through residential proxies, and one operator built a custom skill for proxy use.

According to various reports, DeepSeek v4.1-flash was utilized as the primary model, with GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6 used in additional Claude Code sessions. Models from the DeepSeek Flash family were the most prevalent across the 10 analyzed instances. Note that Operators configured American models on three instances and guardrails triggered only on Anthropic's Opus 5.5. As a consequence in this case, the actor then switched to more permissive Chinese models.

Exploitation in the Wild

Espionage and State-Linked Use

The China-nexus espionage actor VAPOR PANDA ran ARTEX-enabled intrusions for 11 days from October 17, 2026. The campaign targeted more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries, with post-exploitation confirmed at nine. Targets included foreign ministries, a European presidency, and US pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, and nuclear organizations. The operator told the agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor, judged from tasklist output and folder listings.

After access, the actor deployed BLOODALCHEMY through DLL sideloading by a renamed GameHook binary running as svchost.exe. CrowdStrike links the ARTEX controller to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure and distinguishes the campaign from Storm-0940.

Storm-0940, another China-state aligned actor, was responsible for the ConnectWise supply chain compromise. As early as September 2026, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to automate attacks, accelerate scanning and reconnaissance, and attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants.

Incident response engagements since late August 2026 found ARTEX in intrusions at US government, technology, chemicals, and manufacturing organizations. They found artex-probe files, numbered JSP web shells, and webhook.site callback URLs.

CERT-EU reports activity against EU institutions that "highly likely involved the use of ARTEX."

Criminal Campaigns

An analysis of three criminal campaigns using ARTEX found agents operated autonomously after initial goal-setting. These included Apple certificate theft across 10 signing shops, crypto-draining targeting payment infrastructure and TRON wallets, and harvesting over 190,000 gaming credentials. These operations demonstrated low financial barriers and high autonomy, with model costs ranging from $145 to $1,500.

State-linked actors and cybercriminals expanded usage beyond basic pentesting. For instance, VAPOR PANDA targeted over 200 organizations, Storm-0940 used access through a compromised vendor application to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants, and Storm-3358 targeted Southeast Asian financial institutions, all using ARTEX.

Global intelligence advisories, including CERT-In and CERT-EU alerts, emphasize that agentic offensive tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, and Cairn represent a broader shift toward automated, machine-speed exploitation across both espionage and financial attacks.

Why This Matters

ARTEX now serves both espionage and financially motivated actors, enabling them to carry out their attacks at machine speed. The same framework ran intrusions against foreign ministries and defense organizations, sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 tenants, and criminal campaigns that stole signing certificates and gaming accounts. Seeing ARTEX in an intrusion no longer tells defenders who is behind it or what they want.

The skill and money needed to run a campaign have dropped. Operators ran ARTEX in default configurations, and each campaign cost $145 to $1,500 in model time. For less than $1,500, one operator came away with 3 validated signing certificates and their passwords, enough to sign apps that appear to come from the certificate owners.

Exposed weaknesses are found and used faster. The agents retry failed calls within seconds, and in one case of suspected ARTEX use, an agent got from a leaked GitHub secret to Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. A leaked key, an unauthenticated API, or an unpatched internet-facing application can now be found and exploited within minutes.

Trusted paths carry the risk further: one actor turned a compromised vendor application into a launch point against more than 2,250 tenants. One weak link at a vendor or in a delivery pipeline now exposes everyone downstream at machine speed.

Indicator-based defenses lose value against this kind of operator. The agents rotate through residential proxies, and one proxy service showed 79 exit IPs in 100 sampled identities. Behavior on the host and in the cloud stays the same when the addresses change, such as a web server that starts a shell or one app requesting tokens across several services. Coverage gaps are found just as fast: one actor told its agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor.

Attack Chain

The campaigns in this report show the breadth of TTPs that operators run through ARTEX, an agentic penetration testing framework. The same tool served web application exploitation, cloud identity abuse, a vendor supply chain compromise, and espionage implants.

Stage 1: Initial Access

Agents enter through whatever an internet-facing system exposes. In the described criminal campaigns, they used hardcoded administrator passwords, plaintext credential files in the web root, weak administrative credentials, and unauthenticated web APIs. They also exploited IDOR, command injection, and SSTI flaws. A Cambodia-based financially motivated cluster used anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery. A China-state aligned actor abused a compromised multitenant vendor application to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants. In the suspected ARTEX activity against cloud tenants, agents harvested secrets from public GitHub repositories.

Stage 2: Execution and Command and Control

Command injection and SSTI gave the agents code execution in web applications. Agents allegedly used a compromised OAuth application to run scripts on Azure VMs through Run Command against cloud tenants. The financially motivated cluster's agents used curl and netcat to fetch the WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 remote access tools. In attacks against South Korean financial services, operators staged a JNDI/LDAP exploitation rig, and incident responders in other intrusions found numbered JSP web shells and webhook.site callbacks.

Stage 3: Escalation, Discovery, and Evasion

On a Linux host, an agent escalated from a low-privileged user to root through overly permissive folder access. Operator infrastructure also held exploit builds whose file names reference CVE-2022-2588 and CVE-2025-5054. A China-nexus espionage actor told its agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor, judged from tasklist output and folder listings. On the hosts it chose, it sideloaded the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor through a renamed GameHook binary running as svchost.exe. Operators routed agent traffic through residential proxies to rotate their source addresses.

Stage 4: Credential Harvesting

In the suspected ARTEX activity against cloud tenants, agents called Azure operations that return credentials, exfiltrated Key Vault data, and searched Azure DevOps for secrets. In one case, an agent went from a leaked GitHub secret to Key Vault data in five minutes. In AWS, agents searched CloudWatch logs with stolen long-term access keys and self-registered in public Cognito user pools. The criminal campaigns pulled AWS S3 keys from an unauthenticated API and found megabytes of plaintext credentials.

Stage 5: Collection and Monetization

In the suspected ARTEX activity against cloud tenants, agents downloaded SharePoint and OneDrive files and accessed mailbox items. The criminal agents collected more than 300 signing certificates with their passwords and about 6,000 valid gaming accounts, and wrote to an S3 bucket that served a crypto service's iOS apps.

Recommended Mitigations

Find and Rotate Exposed Secrets

Search public GitHub repositories and Azure DevOps for material the agents queried for, such as credentials, application secrets, and AI inference API keys. Rotate every secret you find.

Enable GitHub push protection so new secrets are blocked before they reach a repository.

Close Initial Access Paths

Audit web APIs for responses that return cloud credentials, such as the AWS S3 keys an unauthenticated API leaked in one campaign.

Disable anonymous file upload and fix server-side request forgery flaws on internet-facing systems.

Put administrative interfaces behind a VPN.

Limit the Blast Radius

Review which identities can read storage account keys, App Service settings and publishing credentials, connection strings, AI and ML connections and datastores, and AKS user credentials.

Restrict who can use Run Command on Azure VMs.

Restrict write access to S3 buckets that serve app manifests or landing pages.

Move applications to managed identities where possible, and set app management policies that restrict new secrets and credentials.

Apply least privilege to multi-tenant application permissions.

Watch for Failed Attempts

Alert on Entra ID sign-in errors AADSTS7000215 (invalid secret) and AADSTS7000222 (expired secret). Either one means someone holds a credential for your app. Treat a failure followed by a success as urgent.

Alert on one address authenticating to 3 or more service principals with mixed success, or one app requesting tokens across ARM, Key Vault, Storage, and Graph in a short window.

Alert on a failed API call that is retried shortly after with a different API version, such as the Key Vault rerun about 28 seconds after the first failure.

Alert on user agents that contain artex, the strings Datadog observed in AWS activity.

Block the Indicators

Block the IP addresses and domains in Observed Indicators (Appendix) at the firewall and proxy, and add the SHA-256 hashes to your endpoint blocklist. Treat the Tor exit node, VPN, and proxy addresses as hunting leads rather than blocks, because other traffic shares them. Investigate any historical connection to the indicators.

How SentinelOne Protects Customers

The SentinelOne® agent records what an ARTEX agent does once it reaches a managed host. Behavioral AI detects the shell spawned by a compromised web application, the reconnaissance tools it runs, the escalation to root on a Linux host, and DLL sideloading on a Windows host. Singularity™ AI SIEM correlates Entra ID sign-ins, Azure activity logs, and AWS CloudTrail with that endpoint activity to surface stolen service principal credentials and cloud keys in use. Each step is a hunting point in Purple AI®.

Correlate Identity and Cloud Activity in Singularity AI SIEM

Forward Entra ID sign-in logs, Azure activity logs, Microsoft 365 audit logs, AWS CloudTrail, and web server and WAF logs to Singularity AI SIEM. It ties a failed-then-successful service principal sign-in to the Key Vault, Storage, and Graph token requests the same app makes in a short window. Singularity Identity flags the Entra ID accounts and service principals the actors misuse.

Self-Hosted Customers Should Ensure Known Malicious Hashes Are Blocked

The hunts below find the same activity whatever the hash. Self-hosted customers without cloud reputation services should block every SHA-256 hash in Observed Indicators.

Hunt with Purple AI

Use Purple AI to hunt for the identity and cloud activity described in this report. In Entra ID sign-in logs, Azure activity logs, and AWS CloudTrail forwarded to Singularity AI SIEM, look for service principals that fail with an expired or invalid secret and then sign in successfully, one address signing in to many service principals, unexpected activity by vendor applications such as the affected ConnectWise apps, and requests with artex in the user agent. Look back to August 1, 2026, when the earliest reported activity began.

Use Purple AI to hunt on the endpoint for what an ARTEX agent does after it gets in. On hosts with an active agent, look for web server processes that start a shell, command lines and file paths that contain artx or artex, DLL sideloading by binaries posing as system processes, and connections to the addresses and domains in Observed Indicators. Treat each match as a lead to investigate, because authorized penetration testers also run ARTEX.

articles.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly in Cybersecurity - Week 46 (2026)
articles.context: The Bad | Turla Attackers Deploy Cereal Malware to Spy on Government Exchange Servers Russian state-backed threat group known as Turla is deploying a previously undocumented
articles.full_text:
The Good | Authorities Dismantle Crypto Scams, Ban Illicit Exchange & Seize Malware Infrastructure

Ukrainian law enforcement partnered with German authorities this week to dismantle a network of cryptocurrency scammers that stole over €4.3 million from victims in Europe. Operating out of Ukrainian centers, the criminals used social media and dating apps to carry out romance baiting and other schemes.

After building up trust, they coerced victims into depositing funds into bogus trading platforms and attacker-controlled cryptocurrency wallets. Coordinated raids across four regions yielded hardware wallets, computer equipment, SIM cards, and over $13,000 in seized currencies. The four detained suspects remain in pre-trial custody and face up to 12 years in prison.

In the U.S., the Department of the Treasury cut off MEXC Global cryptocurrency exchange from the American financial system over extensive sanctions evasion and ties to cybercrime gangs. Between 2021 and 2026, the global platform facilitated over $16 billion in illicit transactions, according to an enforcement order from U.S. Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).

Regulators identified MEXC as a key financial clearinghouse for ransomware gangs, darknet activity, and state-backed entities evading sanctions across Russia, Iran, and North Korea. While FinCEN calls out deficiencies in the exchange’s anti-money laundering and customer verification policies, MEXC states they are reviewing the order with legal and compliance experts.

Europol and Eurojust also seized 257 domains and 235 servers powering the Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware operations. The joint takedown, part of the long-running Operation Endgame, spanned nine partner nations all targeting loaders, info-stealers, and remote access trojans (RATs) actively leveraged by cybercriminals to harvest corporate credentials and deploy secondary payloads.

Investigators uncovered over six million compromised credentials and $6.4 million victim datasets stored across the criminal infrastructure. Now, authorities are forwarding the recovered records to public breach-notification services to alert affected organizations and users.

The Bad | Turla Attackers Deploy Cereal Malware to Spy on Government Exchange Servers

Russian state-backed threat group known as Turla is deploying a previously undocumented .NET cyberespionage framework dubbed Cereal to intercept communications on Microsoft Exchange servers across government organizations. Researchers began tracking the first wave of attacks in 2025 when Tulra compromised a government body in Kazakhstan before striking a Romanian state agency. In Romania shortly after, operators configured the toolset to selectively capture sensitive email correspondence involving representatives from NATO and the European Union.

Turla (aka Snake, UNC4210), linked to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), engineered Cereal for stealthy, long-term intelligence gathering. The malware avoids external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure entirely. Instead, it abuses the compromised Exchange server itself as a centralized execution hub and persistent collection point. The framework comprises eight modular components that rely extensively on data serialization and in-memory execution to conceal illicit activity from security defenders.

A primary module, named CerealBox, injects directly into Exchange's transport service process, EdgeTransport.exe. Once inside, it hijacks existing transport handlers to inspect message traffic without registering unauthorized transport agents or interrupting normal email delivery. The module automatically compresses, encrypts, and stages messages containing PDF, DOC, or DOCX attachments matching targeted sender, recipient, or subject criteria.

At the same time, a passive backdoor named CerealNeuron listens for incoming encrypted web requests designed to blend with regular Exchange traffic. Upon receiving instructions, it launches disposable CerealRunner binaries that execute memory-resident payloads to query Active Directory, extract LSA secrets, inspect mailboxes, and return encrypted results to the backdoor for exfiltration.

Security analysts emphasize that Cereal's extensive concealment strategies reflect Turla’s deep understanding of .NET execution techniques running inside legitimate processes, marking a mature offensive platform ready for long-term, stealthy cyberespionage.

The Ugly | Threat Actors Breach Railway Infrastructure to Steal Customer AI Secrets

Cloud hosting platform Railway confirmed that threat actors exploited flaws within its build infrastructure to steal decrypted customer authentication secrets, resulting in an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized AI usage charges.

The intrusion began on October 20 when adversaries exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to escape build filesystem isolation and capture internal credentials. Using these credentials, the attackers accessed stored build histories and obtained a copy of Railway's monorepo source code to identify further exploitation paths across the environment.

The attackers then exploited an improperly configured OIDC trust binding within Railway's cloud deployment system, moving laterally to compromise an orchestration server. Since that machine managed fleet workloads, it held credentials authorized to decrypt customer environment variables via cloud key management services.

Between October 20 and October 21, the intrusion escalated into a 26-hour operational contest between Railway engineers and threat actors deploying autonomous AI agents to probe systems in parallel.

Forensic investigations revealed that the attackers specifically targeted environment variables containing API keys for major AI providers, likely seeking access for resale or model distillation. The breach potentially exposed credentials across at most 1.85% of workspaces, representing approximately 100,000 customer environments, alongside linked-account tokens for 1,852 users. However, forensic analysis showed no evidence that attackers accessed customer databases. The investigation also found no indication that attackers downloaded private Git repositories.

Railway fully evicted the threat actors on October 21, isolated each build within dedicated ephemeral virtual machines, and rotated affected tokens. While the company is coordinating with AI providers to secure customer refunds, it pledged to cover any fraudulent charges that vendors decline to reimburse.

#on-call #alerts-ci #deploy-watch #support-escalations

Connectors

GitHub, GitLab, Sentry, dbt, PagerDuty, Linear, Datadog, Jira, Grafana, incident.io

Threads and routines

Incident response, morning incident digest, Monday on-call handoff, daily health summary, hourly incident recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: monitor alerts and immediately triage each one in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket. Query the data first, then theorize, and separate what you verified from what you inferred. If it's real, name the likely root cause with links, tag the owner, and open a draft PR only if the fix is contained. If no action is needed, say so. After each incident, add what you learned to [lessons file].

Triage channels are notoriously noisy. There are constant interruptions from Sentry errors, Datadog alerts, customer bug reports, and support requests making it difficult to find the signal from noise. It's usually the first task teams hand to Claude.

With Claude in the channel as a first responder, the first pass is often done before the on-call engineer opens their laptop. Claude reads each item as it lands, investigates the codebase and the tools it has access to, and shares what it found. If the fix is contained, it opens a draft PR; if not, it routes the issue to the right person with the investigation attached. In these setups, a person reviews each fix before it merges, and only genuinely new problems need someone to start the investigation themselves.

At Campfire, which builds an AI-native ERP for finance teams, an engineer tagged Claude on a report that some of its AI agent’s finished answers weren’t reaching users. Claude had a PR open 21 minutes later, and it merged that afternoon.

Kikoff: A first responder in every triage channel

Kikoff is a fintech startup that helps consumers build credit, solve liquidity needs, and achieve financial security. Claude Tag is the first responder in triage channels across the company, including:

#deploys: Claude decides what to watch after each release and flags anything it broke.

#alerts-ci: When a build fails, Claude finds out why and proposes a fix as a draft PR.

#alerts-sentry-backend: Claude takes the first pass on Sentry exceptions and crashes.

#dog-fooding: Claude investigates what employees flag while dogfooding and tags the right owner.

#support: Claude takes the first pass on support tickets.

Kikoff started with Claude contributing to the conversation only when mentioned, and the biggest wins came once the team let it jump in on its own. When sign-up broke, Claude traced it to a backend change, sized the impact, named the team that owned the fix, and opened a draft PR so the app would fail softly in the meantime.

“I’m always hyped when Claude catches an issue before a monitor or human does. One person can only personally manage so much context, Claude Tag helps us organize and own some context, and we manage the outcomes.”

NavigateAI: Fixing bugs with fragmented context

NavigateAI builds AI copilots for construction field teams. They run Claude Tag in about 90 channels for alert triage, bug bashes, quick feature building, and support escalations. Since June, Claude has opened about 223 PRs straight from Slack threads and 134 have merged with a median of two hours from open to merge.

Triage has been a particularly valuable use case for NavigateAI. Because Claude has so much context, it can find unintuitive root causes to issues that may have been missed at first glance.

“Our biggest ‘wow!’ moment with Claude Tag was when we were trying to debug a load issue, which seemed to be caused by a customer (since their calls were failing). A normal human response would be to continue chasing down that customer. But because Claude had access to so many other data sources, it actually found that it was from an uninstrumented internal cron job that was running during the same time.”

With Claude, mean time to resolve issues has improved. In one case, Claude had the root cause eight minutes after a Sentry alert fired, and the fix was merged 93 minutes after the alert.

“Fast-moving startups typically have to pick speed over structure. Claude Tag gives us both. It’s a brain that connects the dots across all our tools, so we get the structure without having to build it ourselves,” said Mike.

02 Thread to PR

Example setups:

Channels

#quick-wins #bug-bash #product-feedback #feature-requests #ux-papercuts #tech-debt #design-polish

Connectors

GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Notion, Figma, Sentry

Threads and routines

One request per thread, weekly backlog sweep, daily PR roundup, weekly shipped recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: when someone describes a bug or small feature, work on it in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket and read the related code first. If details are missing, ask for them or for a real example instead of guessing. If the change is small and contained, open a draft PR with a short summary of what changed and how you tested it. Never merge; a person reviews and approves. If it's too big or risky, say why and suggest a ticket.

Speed is one of a startup’s biggest advantages, but often small requests that delight users can get lost in the shuffle. The intelligence is often gathered by customer-facing teams, submitted in Slack, and, if it's not overlooked, eventually makes its way to Linear or Jira where it’s prioritized against hundreds of other tickets.

With Claude Tag, anyone can draft the PR, technical or not. Surface an idea in a thread, get live feedback from product, engineering, and GTM in the same place, and Claude turns the thread into a draft PR that reflects everyone’s input.

Many of the startups we spoke with used Claude Tag for the “light and delight” features or to remove papercuts that are quick to review but would otherwise not get prioritized.

Orderful: From Slack exchange to production feature in two days

Orderful is an EDI platform that connects companies with their trading partners, through an API or straight from the browser. Its customers trade standard documents with their partners through the platform.

One document type, the 753, wasn’t supported in Orderful’s web app. The request had sat in the backlog, and shipments for one large retailer were delayed.

When an account manager followed up in Slack, the PM tagged Claude in: “@Claude, you should build one.” Claude asked for real examples of the document so it could build to the actual format, then opened a draft PR adding 753 support.

The next morning, Claude filed a ticket for the accompanying 754, the retailer’s response, and opened a second PR. Both were in production about two days after the Slack exchange.

“Something that took weeks or months before just took a Slack conversation,” said Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful. “Light features with hard-to-prove value used to get stuck in the backlog. Now they have a way out.”

Valence: From feature request to rollout

Valence works with the world’s largest employers to connect enterprise talent and performance with Nadia, an AI coach. When a Valence engineer explained in Slack how to address an urgent product change requested by an important client, Claude didn’t just follow directions, it identified additional changes that needed to be made as the same configuration lived in two spots. Without Claude, the initial change would have been incomplete.

“It didn’t just agree with the expert. It caught duplicated configuration, the kind of thing humans lose track of.”

In another case, a client urgently asked for a customization. Claude checked the code and, working with an engineer, confirmed it could ship with no code change. In under an hour, a teammate had a solution ready for the client.

03 Company brain

Example setups:

Channels

#ask-anything #company-wiki #product-questions

Connectors

GitHub, Notion, Google Drive, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Granola, Metabase

Threads and routines

One question per thread, decision log updates, weekly stale doc check, repeat questions recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: answer questions from our code, docs and past threads, and link your sources. If sources disagree, check the code, give the current answer, and flag the stale doc. If you aren’t sure, say so and tag the owner. When a thread reaches a decision, record it in [docs location]. Anything going to a client needs a human check first.

At a startup, institutional knowledge often lives in people's heads, from the intricacies of product billing codes to where the onboarding docs are hosted.

For many of the startups we spoke with, Claude Tag has become the company brain. Claude answers with the source, and tags the owner when it isn't confident. It keeps that knowledge current too: when a thread reaches a decision, Claude can record it in your docs the same day and flag docs that have gone stale.

Moritz: A live source of truth from intake to staffing

Moritz is an AI-native law firm that promises a same-day turnaround on contracts, against what Moritz cites as an industry standard of at least three weeks. Everything around the legal work, from intake and quoting to staffing and follow-up, lives in Slack, with a thread per matter and a channel per client.

Now everyone from the CEO to paralegals asks Claude first. Questions that took up to 30 minutes of searching in Slack get answered in under two. The end-of-shift update, now drafted from the day’s threads, went from about an hour of assembly to a five-minute edit.

That time goes back to legal work. Claude Tag handles the administrative work around a case, like follow-up questions, reminders, and status updates. It can’t access client documents or privileged conversations with Moritz’s lawyers.

“A firm working across 44 countries generates hundreds of one-off questions a month that no one will ever build a feature for. Claude Tag answers them from our own history in Slack. Every answer is a thread with links, so institutional memory compounds.”

Campfire: Customer experience on demand

One Slack channel in particular “exploded in popularity”: their CX (or customer experience) channel. Sales uses this channel “to validate certain functionality during prospect conversations,” rather than having to “ping 10 different people.”

This type of channel is particularly effective because sales can answer in the moment, while the customer is paying attention, and can operate more independently and confidently in early customer conversations.

“Claude Tag basically acts as our central knowledge base.”

04 Self-serve data

Example setups:

Channels

#data-requests #ask-revops #metric-definitions

Connectors

dbt, GitHub, Metabase, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, Notion

Threads and routines

One question per thread, weekly pre-standup readout, launch and experiment readouts, pipeline failure triage, new question triage

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: answer from our governed models and the definitions in [data skills repo]. If the data isn’t covered there, say it’s unvalidated instead of guessing. Lead with the answer, then give the number, what’s driving it, and any caveat. Check recent incidents, releases, and Slack discussions before explaining a change. If a metric’s definition is unclear, ask which one we mean. For anything important, share your plan or SQL before you run it. Separate what you verified from what you assumed, and list any open data quality warnings at the end of your answer. If someone finds a mistake, draft a fix for a data team member to review. If a question comes up twice, suggest scheduling it.

At a fast-growing startup every function wants numbers, and the data team has to decide whose request comes first. With Claude Tag connected to your data, anyone can ask in plain English without waiting in the data team’s queue.

This is a use case we have adopted as well. In one of our data channels over a month, Claude Tag answered more than 75% of questions people posted, typically within a minute or two. It works from governed data and the same definitions analysts use, which live in a versioned repo that Claude re-reads in every conversation.

Descript: Answering ad-hoc data requests

Descript is an AI-powered video editing platform. Claude Tag is now the first line of support for data requests and initial analyses. Product, growth, RevOps, and finance ask questions in Slack and get answers grounded in Descript’s dbt models.

“I used to write complicated SQL and refresh the numbers by hand every week or month. Now I’ve replaced several data-team dashboards with my own Claude artifacts, and I no longer refresh them by hand.”

Daisy’s recurring reporting prep went from days to hours.

The growth team, for example, asks why lifecycle subscriptions dropped, whether paid search is losing last-touch credit to other channels, or how long a self-serve account takes to become an enterprise opportunity. The data team tracks the artifacts Claude generates to see which data assets matter most across teams, and spends its own time on strategic questions and on building the context that makes self-serve work.

“The promise of business intelligence has always been self-serve for business users. I’d never seen it actually realized until we had Claude Tag set up with immense context for our data.”

Orderful: From question to dashboard

At Orderful, self-serve analytics spans conversational analytics and full data builds: anyone can go from a question in Slack to a dashboard merged to production. The key is a semantic layer that encodes agreed definitions and metrics, so every answer and every build uses the same definitions.

“We trust the output because a semantic layer constrains the SQL, CI gates the builds, and there’s a process for agreeing on definitions. Without those, you get confident-looking wrong answers. Once those guardrails were in place, connecting Claude Tag took under 30 minutes. Now teammates build together in shared Slack threads instead of solo sessions.”

05 Reporting and handoffs

Example setups:

Channels

#sales-pipeline #customer-handoffs #standup-summary #qbr-prep

Connectors

Notion, Google Drive, Gong, Salesforce, Gainsight

Threads and routines

End-of-day status draft, pre-QBR brief, deal handoff

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: draft each recurring report from our threads, docs, and data, and link your sources. Lead with what changed and what needs a decision. Separate what you verified from what you assumed, and flag anything missing instead of filling the gap. Post the draft in its own thread for [owner] to edit. Nothing goes out until a person approves it. If a report keeps getting the same edits, suggest updating these instructions.

Many of the examples we’ve covered are reactive: something happens, Claude responds. Routine reporting is work Claude owns on a schedule, the way a teammate owns a recurring deliverable.

You describe the outcome once; Claude runs it every time and posts the result where the team already works.

Valence: Deal reviews and handoffs

Valence is setting Claude up to brief the team before every quarterly business review, with customer health, open deals, blockers, and next steps. They are also working to make the handoff from sales to customer success when a deal closes more seamless. Claude saves the team time by helping to aggregate details across their engagement and often finds key items they may have missed.

“When a deal closes, Tag builds the handoff from the deal history, calls and contract: who’s who, what was promised, what’s customized, and what’s still open. Customer success then reviews it before their kickoff,” said Sameer.

06 Getting started checklist

The checklist below pulls together these startup teams’ best practices so you can apply them to your own workflows.

Before launch

Check the prerequisites.

Claude Tag is in public beta on Claude Team and Enterprise plans, and isn’t available on Free, Pro, or Max. You’ll need a Claude organization Owner and a Slack workspace admin to connect the two. An admin must also turn on Routines, and Team plans need usage credits before Claude responds.

Set up Claude’s access with a bundle.

In channels, Claude works under its own agent identity, with service accounts rather than anyone’s personal login. Group the connectors, repos, and instructions it needs in a bundle, and attach them org-wide, per workspace, or per channel. That sets what Claude can reach in each place, and everyone in a channel gets the same access. Start narrow: only what the first channel’s job needs.

Experiment in a private channel.

Nearly half the startups we spoke with started their Claude Tag journey by having a small cross-functional team experiment in a private channel. “Start private with a mix of roles, then move to a group channel,” said Sameer.

Determine the boundaries.

By default, anyone in your Slack workspace can use Claude, even without a Claude account. You can restrict access to your org and limit search to channels Claude is in. On Enterprise, you can also restrict access to specific roles or chosen channels.

Set clear expectations for what Claude can do and can never do. Several teams we spoke with let Claude open draft PRs, but people review and merge. For Orderful, Claude Code, not Tag, handles “infrastructure changes, audits, sensitive data.” For a “hard call,” such as “a PR that touches more than one service,” Claude gets a second opinion. Moritz doesn’t give Claude Tag access to client documents or privileged conversations with its lawyers.

Start your security review early.

The usual questions are data retention and what Claude can reach, and the security and data lifecycle pages answer both. Claude Tag isn’t available to orgs with zero data retention turned on, a customer-managed encryption (CMEK) policy, or the HIPAA configuration, and it isn’t covered by our Business Associate Agreement, so check that before you plan a rollout.

Set a budget and alerts.

Claude Tag bills by usage, so an early conversation avoids surprises as adoption grows. You can set spend limits overall and per channel, choose the model per channel, and attribute costs by user using the Enterprise Analytics API. Orderful runs an org-wide cap with alerts at 75% and 90%. “We have extreme ownership on the channel costs. The owner justifies that ‘yes, this spend is reasonable for the output / outcomes,’” said Alex Dejeu, engineering manager at Kikoff. Use your first channel’s actual costs to size the next one.

Deployment

Pick one clear task in a channel your team already uses, like on-call alerts or bug triage.

“We experiment on certain teams, see what works, then once confident we’ve worked out the kinks, we push the idea out to other teams to add to their own similar channels as well. We want to avoid trust breaking experiences with folks with lower tolerance to AI mistakes,” said Alex Dejeu, engineering manager at Kikoff.

Prime your experts and culture bearers.

Have the people your team already trusts use Claude first, and in the open.

“Going back and forth with Claude in the open has been productive and fun. Several people in sales and customer success have watched experts [interact with Claude Tag], then started asking Claude themselves, and got value fast,” said Sameer Bansal, principal AI engineer at Valence.

Tune the noise.

Multiple startups told us they needed to adjust Claude’s chattiness. Too chatty is one risk.

“Conversation in ad hoc requests can sometimes get noisy. We’ve been trying to tune down the responsiveness here and also be more principled on what we use Claude on ad hoc requests for,” said Mike Chen, head of engineering at NavigateAI.

Too little chattiness is also a risk, however. In busy channels, “You either have to @ every time or it won’t do much,” said Will Hu, cofounder at Flagler Health. And “if no one is watching a channel closely or interacts with it, it will sit idle.”

Have teammates connect their own accounts.

The admin bundles from setup are what Claude can reach for everyone in a channel. Personal connectors work differently: Claude acts with the permissions of the person asking, so it can pull from their docs, inbox, or CRM once they approve it (an Owner adds the connector for the org first, and on Enterprise an admin manages personal connectors). The answer still posts in the channel, so choose “Allow with review” for anything sensitive.

Write channel instructions like you’re onboarding a new hire:

what to check first, when to open a PR, when to ask, and that “no action needed” is a valid answer.

Give Claude feedback in the channel, not in DMs.

Correct it in the thread. It remembers per channel, and teammates learn how to work with it by watching. For a lasting fix, ask Claude to update its memory for this channel.

Not sure where to go next? Tag Claude and ask what it has learned about your org and which use cases it would expand to.

Moritz’s co-founder and CTO, Stefan Mandaric, asked Claude to recommend use cases for each team. Fifteen minutes later, it had read the firm’s Slack channels, Linear issues, Notion SOPs, Drive, and Metabase dashboards, and published 25. “18 of 25 worked with no further setup. That became our rollout plan.”

Last word: what we learned from the wow moments

The wow moments weren’t always about speed. Often, Claude found something no one had asked it to look for. Sometimes the surprise was restraint. And sometimes the surprise was the unexpected exchanges. “Eventually you get used to Claude jumping in on jokes, and you soon appreciate that it’s an easy audience and the first one to laugh,” said Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful.

We hope you found this guide useful. Special thanks to Campfire, Descript, Flagler Health, Kikoff, Moritz, NavigateAI, Orderful and Valence for sharing their experiences and insights.

articles.title: LABScon26 Replay | Let’s Get Physical: Why Cybersecurity Needs Hardware-Based Security to Survive AI

articles.full_text:
In his LABScon 26 keynote, Dino Dai Zovi, SVP and Head of Security at Adyen, argues that defenders can’t keep pace with AI-enabled attackers through software alone. He makes the case that the hardware-based security already protecting everyday payments can close that gap.

Using tap-to-pay as an example, Dai Zovi notes how a secure element in a smartphone completes a transaction that malware on the device cannot touch. At the same time, data from the UK’s AI Security Institute on autonomous cyber capability shows end-to-end intrusions that once took days or months are now approaching minutes, with open-weight models only months behind frontier models.

Arguing that the main risk from AI is not AI agents turning on humanity but humans using AI to achieve malicious goals, Dai Zovi proposes engineering for resilience using hardware-based controls. He draws on analogies with bank vaults and nuclear weapon safety principles to show how hardware controls have long contained risks that would otherwise depend on people or software behaving correctly. He then works through an AI cyber range on the assumption that none of its vulnerabilities can be patched, and shows how a handful of hardware boundaries leave an agent with nothing useful to take.

He closes with a question. If the technology to contain AI already runs at scale in systems used many times a day, should we choose to apply it?

This presentation is essential viewing for security engineers, architects and leaders thinking about how to defend against AI-accelerated attacks.

About the Author

Dino Dai Zovi is SVP and Head of Security at Adyen. He previously served as Head of Applied Security Engineering at Block, where he led security for Cash App and for Square’s expansion into EMV card payments, including the work that inspired the PCI SPoC mobile PIN entry standard. He is best known for winning the first Pwn2Own contest in 2007, co-authoring “The iOS Hacker’s Handbook” and “The Mac Hacker’s Handbook,” and co-founding Trail of Bits, Capsule8 and the Pwnie Awards.

About LABScon

This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS.

articles.full_text:
Researchers been able to take over customer accounts at two car brands. They then demonstrated how they could remotely unlock and start a test car after finding an administration console on the brands' login servers still protected by its default password.

Security researchers Shubham Shah and Sam Curry detailed the work in a write-up published November 7. Customer logins for both brands ran on OpenIDM, identity management software from ForgeRock, now part of Ping Identity. The brands were not named, at the automakers' request.

The researchers reported the flaw to the two automakers and pointed to ForgeRock's hardening guidance to remove or protect the console before deployment.

Test Car Unlocked and Started From a Hijacked Account

In early 2026, the researchers bypassed the web application firewall (WAF) in front of the login servers and found the console still accepted its documented default credentials. From there they ran their own code on the identity servers and changed the email address and password on a test account.

Logging in as that customer through the normal app, they unlocked and started the test car with its owner present. The session also exposed the vehicle's location and telemetry.

The researchers wrote that they could have created a session for any customer account on the affected deployments. Changing an account's login details also left the owner's existing app session active, and the researchers could divert the app's notifications away from the owner's phone.

Both automakers fixed the issue about two hours after the flaw was reported and rotated affected credentials, according to the write-up.

Read more on default passwords in connected systems: CISA, FBI Urge Action to Protect Industrial Refrigeration Networks

Australian Systems Exposed Through Hardcoded Credentials

In a companion post, Shah described a separate chain against one of the automaker's Australian systems, researched in July 2026.

The chain could start from a car's number plate. Hardcoded administrator credentials, a WAF bypass and a misconfigured multi-factor authentication (MFA) step then allowed account takeover and remote unlocking.

The exposed data included customers' names, phone numbers and password hashes. Together, the write-ups covered vehicles in Australia, the US and Canada. The researchers wrote that they tested only on cars they owned or had permission to use.

Shah's post does not say when the Australian findings were reported or whether they have been fixed. Neither post reports malicious use or says whether the researchers checked for it.

articles.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly in Cybersecurity - Week 45 (2026)
articles.context: Once connected, attackers instructed victims to launch Quick Assist, a built-in Windows remote-help tool, and read back connection codes to grant full remote desktop control
articles.full_text:
The Good | Global Authorities Dismantle Investment Scams & VasyGrek Infrastructure, Indict University System Hackers

Law enforcement in Europe, supported by Europol and Eurojust, arrested seven suspects and seized over 100 servers targeting a crime-as-a-service (CaaS) investment fraud infrastructure. Operating from Cyprus and Israel, an unnamed vendor supplied fraudulent trading websites to criminal call centers across Albania, Kosovo, North Macedonia, and more.

Following a four-year investigation initiated after victims reported missing funds, investigators linked the infrastructure to fake foreign currency, stock, and cryptocurrency schemes affecting victims in at least 50 countries. Scammers used fake online account profits to coerce larger transfers before cutting contact, leaving victims unable to recover their funds.

In the U.S., a federal grand jury indicted two Canadian nationals, Ryan James Roach and Mathiew James Stubbings, for conspiring to breach multiple American universities to mine for cryptocurrency. Between June 2016 and December 2019, the co-conspirators deployed virtual private servers to infect academic networks across Massachusetts, New York, North Carolina, and Tennessee with malware.

Once inside, the defendants stole user log-ins and data, deployed cryptocurrency mining software, and hijacked high-performance campus supercomputers to conduct unauthorized network vulnerability research. Both men face up to ten years in prison and $250,000 fines following formal extradition proceedings from Canada.

Russian law enforcement authorities arrested three suspected members of the VasyGrek threat group (aka Fluffy Wolf) and dismantled its operational infrastructure. Active since 2016, the financially-motivated group was known for targeting organizations across metallurgy, energy, healthcare, and finance sectors in Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan.

Attackers would send phishing emails with malicious accounting attachments to drop remote access trojans and steal corporate funds. Police seized computer equipment and server assets after uncovering a broad network of fake financial domains, dark web remote administration tools, and Golang backdoors used to execute unauthorized commands.

The Bad | Impersonators Abuse Microsoft Teams and Active Directory Certificate Services

According to a new report, threat actors have been posing as IT help desk staff on Microsoft Teams to message and call corporate employees and leverage external support-themed tenants to trick users into handing over workstation access.

Once connected, attackers instructed victims to launch Quick Assist, a built-in Windows remote-help tool, and read back connection codes to grant full remote desktop control. The intruders then dropped malicious software archives into Downloads folders, unpacking and executing payloads via portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes disguised as legitimate Windows system updates.

After establishing initial persistence, the attackers abused weak configuration templates within Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) to request digital authentication certificates for privileged domain accounts. In one documented intrusion, threat actors exploited an ESC1 misconfiguration to obtain certificates for three highly privileged identities—access that persisted even after password resets or workstation wipes. The attacker used one of those certificates to compromise a domain controller, execute DCSync credential dumping, and exfiltrate internal corporate files to an external server via Rclone.

In a second intrusion, attackers targeted an ESC8 configuration by deploying the ‘PetitPotam’ technique to force a domain controller to authenticate against an attacker-controlled endpoint. The relayed NTLM authentication allowed the actors to request a certificate directly for the domain controller without credentials, securing a persistent Kerberos ticket-granting ticket. The customer isolated the affected workstation, and no further attack progression was observed.

Because these intrusions exploit misconfigured certificate enrollment policies rather than underlying software vulnerabilities, Microsoft advises organizations to confirm unexpected support requests via internal channels, enforce Extended Protection for Authentication on web enrollment endpoints, and audit certificate issuance rules.

The Ugly | Threat Actors Disrupt European Refrigeration Systems Across Retail and Healthcare Sectors

Threat actors have targeted internet-exposed refrigeration control systems across Europe this week, altering temperature settings and activating defrost cycles across facilities just three weeks after similar attacks on hundreds of refrigeration systems in French supermarkets.

So far, this second wave has impacted retail chains across Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Sweden. In several stores, attackers set cooling units to generate heat or raised temperature setpoints to 50°C.

The activity extended into critical healthcare infrastructure when a cyberattack on refrigeration supplier Coolworld Rentals raised temperature thresholds at French Blood Establishment (EFS) cold-storage facilities managing vital blood supplies. However, automated monitoring alarms enabled staff to relocate stored blood products before any inventory was lost.

SentinelLABS’s breakdown notes that similar attacks targeted Israeli and Russian facilities in 2022, a Los Angeles meat processor in 2024, and U.S. military commissaries in August 2026. The intrusions primarily targeted commercial supervisory platforms, such as Danfoss AK-SM, AK-SC, and Copeland Dixell XWEB controllers, that centralize site cooling operations.

At the time, ANSSI indicated that adversaries gained control by exploiting publicly accessible administration interfaces and weak default credentials rather than executing novel software zero-days.

While Russian-aligned hacktivist collectives including CARR, NoName057(16), and Z-Pentest claimed responsibility for specific disruptions, law enforcement authorities have not formally confirmed attribution. Opportunistic scanning against unhardened building management systems allows multiple threat groups to execute similar disruptions.

To mitigate ongoing operational risks, government advisories from CERT-FR instruct operators to immediately disconnect exposed control panels from the public internet, restrict remote maintenance access to secure virtual private networks, enforce strong authentication controls, and replace legacy end-of-life hardware.

articles.title: Cyber Resilience Starts with AI Governance
articles.context: It can improve operational efficiency and enable faster threat detection and response
articles.full_text:
Today’s cybercriminals are increasingly using AI to scale, accelerate, and evolve their attacks. At the same time, organizations are recognizing that AI can be a powerful force for defense, using it to strengthen cybersecurity, improve security operations, and protect networks at machine speed.

Data in the Fortinet 2026 Cybersecurity Skills Gap Report confirms the near-ubiquity of this response, with 91% of the IT leaders in the 2,700+ organizations surveyed stating they are using or exploring the use of AI-empowered cybersecurity solutions. Unfortunately, as we move higher up the corporate ladder, only 50% of respondents believe their boards of directors fully comprehend the cybersecurity vulnerabilities associated with AI. This disconnect highlights a governance gap, which creates risk for the organization.

Why Boards of Directors Need to Fully Understand AI

To defend against AI-powered criminals, organizations need to build cyber resilience, but they can’t do that if leadership doesn't understand AI and its potential risks. That gap becomes even more significant as AI-driven defenses become more embedded within organizations. As AI adoption accelerates, company-wide AI literacy and cybersecurity governance must evolve alongside it.

According to the Fortinet 2026 Cybersecurity Skills Gap Report, although nearly three-quarters of respondents say their boards view cybersecurity as a business priority, only 59% say that priority is reflected in spending decisions. This discrepancy suggests many organizations recognize the importance of cybersecurity in principle but struggle to translate that awareness into sustained investment and governance.

The report also highlights what's at stake for leadership. Half of organizations say board members or senior executives faced personal consequences following a cyberattack, including fines, loss of employment, or other penalties. As cyber risk increasingly becomes business risk, executive oversight has never been more important.

AI-Informed Leadership Teams

Board members don’t need to become AI engineers. But they do need enough understanding of AI to ask the right questions, evaluate risk, and provide effective oversight.

AI literacy also shouldn’t stop with the boardroom or the security team. IT staff, software developers, and business leaders also need a foundational understanding of how AI systems work, the risks they pose, and how to mitigate those risks.

For boards and C-suite leaders, education should focus on governance, risk oversight, executive accountability, policies, investment decisions, and regulatory implications. With a shared knowledge base across the organization, leaders can better balance the productivity and security benefits of AI with its potential risks.

The goal is an AI-informed leadership team that can balance AI's potential with its risks and make informed decisions about adoption, investment, and governance.

What Should Organizations Do Today to Build AI Literacy?

Organizations should begin by assessing their current AI readiness and identifying knowledge gaps across leadership, security teams, IT, and the broader workforce.

An organization’s board of directors must understand the benefits that come with AI adoption. First, AI can act as a force multiplier for short-handed IT security teams. It can improve operational efficiency and enable faster threat detection and response. But leadership must also recognize that realizing these benefits requires people with the skills to securely manage, oversee, and govern AI-enabled environments.

Organizations can address these challenges through a combination of governance, workforce education, and structured skills development. Programs that provide AI education and cybersecurity certification can help employees build the knowledge needed to use, secure, and responsibly manage AI.

The Fortinet Training Institute can help your organization acquire AI literacy and workforce education. Training programs are designed to support the acquisition of technical expertise across leadership, security teams, and the broader workforce.

AI is already changing how organizations defend themselves. The next step is ensuring the people responsible for guiding that transformation understand both its opportunities and its risks.

As organizations strengthen AI governance, another workforce challenge comes into focus: finding and developing professionals with the skills to secure, manage, and govern increasingly AI-enabled environments.
