articles.title: GitHub to Block pull_request_target Workflows by Default Starting December 2
articles.context: A malicious contributor can exploit those mistakes to execute commands with access to credentials and other resources intended only for trusted automation
articles.full_text:
GitHub will begin blocking GitHub Actions workflows triggered by pull_request_target in public repositories on December 2, 2026, expanding its protections against a class of CI/CD vulnerabilities that has repeatedly enabled attackers to steal credentials and compromise open source software releases.

The restriction, originally announced in September, will prevent affected workflows from running unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them. GitHub had initially scheduled enforcement for November 2 but confirmed the postponed December 2 deadline in a new update this week, giving maintainers additional time to review their automation and configure exceptions.

The new restriction goes beyond protections introduced in June, when GitHub updated actions/checkout to prevent common attempts to check out untrusted pull request code inside privileged workflows. This time, GitHub is blocking the pull_request_target trigger itself by default, including for workflows that use it safely.

pull_request_target Is Now a Common Attack Vector Vector #

GitHub introduced pull_request_target in 2020 to help maintainers automate tasks involving pull requests from external contributors. Unlike the standard pull_request event, which restricts access to secrets and provides a read-only token for contributions from forks, pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository with access to its configured secrets and token permissions.

That elevated access makes the trigger useful for legitimate maintenance tasks such as assigning reviewers, labeling pull requests, and posting authenticated comments. The workflow definition runs from the repository's trusted default branch, rather than the contributor's proposed changes.

The security risk emerges when that privileged workflow checks out and executes code from an untrusted fork or passes attacker-controlled pull request data into shell commands. A malicious contributor can exploit those mistakes to execute commands with access to credentials and other resources intended only for trusted automation.

Researchers have warned about these vulnerabilities, commonly called "pwn requests," since at least 2021. Variations of this attack pattern contributed to major supply chain incidents involving Nx, PostHog, and TanStack.

GitHub's June changes addressed a common source of these vulnerabilities by making actions/checkout reject unsafe fork checkouts in privileged workflows unless explicitly overridden. The December policy takes a broader approach, preventing the event from triggering a workflow at all unless administrators have authorized it through an applicable policy.

Two Test Windows Before December Enforcement #

GitHub's default restriction currently operates in evaluation mode, allowing affected workflows to continue running before enforcement begins.

The company has scheduled two temporary enforcement periods, known as brownouts, to expose configurations that will stop working under the new policy:

November 9, 16:00–18:00 UTC

November 16, 16:00–18:00 UTC

During those windows, blocked pull_request_target attempts will generate failed workflow runs with an error annotation instead of executing. The default policy will return to evaluation mode after each test.

On December 2, the restriction becomes permanent for affected public repositories without an applicable policy allowing the event. The change applies to public repositories on GitHub Free, Team, and Enterprise Cloud, but excludes private and internal repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server.

Maintainers who still require pull_request_target can create an Actions event policy that explicitly permits it. GitHub supports targeting individual workflow files, allowing administrators to preserve specific automation without enabling the trigger across an entire repository. Existing applicable event policies are not replaced by the new default.

Some Open Source Maintainers Face a Complicated Transition #

The broader restriction introduces complications for open source projects that have relied on pull_request_target for legitimate automation, sometimes across dozens of repositories.

A carefully configured workflow that only labels pull requests or manages project metadata may pose little of the risk GitHub is addressing, but it will still be subject to the new restriction. Maintainers must either allow these workflows explicitly or move them to another trigger where appropriate.

There are also differences in the administrative tools available across GitHub's pricing tiers.

GitHub's documentation for workflow execution protections describes policy configuration at the repository, organization, and enterprise levels for public repositories, including those on free plans. However, the ability to create policies in evaluation mode is reserved for Enterprise Cloud, where administrators can examine policy insights before turning on enforcement.

That disparity had already prompted questions following GitHub's September announcement of the new defaults.

In a GitHub Community discussion, open source maintainer George Joseph questioned how smaller organizations were expected to assess the impact without Enterprise policy insights.

"How would us mere mortals who run open-source organizations see what workflows would be affected?" he asked.

A community response suggested manually searching repositories for workflows using pull_request_target, inspecting existing workflow runs, and testing explicit allowlisting policies. These approaches can identify affected configurations, but require additional work from maintainers managing multiple repositories.

The December deadline gives projects several more weeks to prepare, while the scheduled brownouts offer a preview of what enforcement will look like. GitHub's decision also represents a significant shift for a feature originally created to make external contributions easier to manage: privileged pull request automation will now require an explicit exception to continue running under the new default.

articles.title: VerifiedIDA | Making LLM-Driven Reverse Engineering Inspectable, Continuable and Reusable
articles.context: In cybersecurity, for example, defenders can analyze larger volumes of malware in less time, while attackers can misuse the same capability to considerably accelerate and scale...
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

SentinelLABS evaluated how frontier models reverse engineer binaries and annotate disassembler databases, finding recurring problems with inaccurate labels and incomplete analysis.

To improve performance, we developed and tested a standard for LLM-driven reverse engineering that keeps annotations tied to evidence, verifies database changes, preserves project state, and requires review of the model’s work.

We open-sourced VerifiedIDA, a reference implementation that applies the standard to autonomous reverse engineering in IDA Pro.

Despite the growing capabilities of new models, our research shows that scaling reverse engineering requires that the analysis they produce remain inspectable, continuable, and reusable by humans, other models, and downstream security workflows.

Overview

The use of large language models (LLMs) for reverse engineering creates the possibility of examining binaries at a scale and speed exceeding that of manual analysis. It also makes reverse engineering accessible to those without specialized expertise in the discipline. The combination of scale, speed, and accessibility introduces a major shift across multiple domains. In cybersecurity, for example, defenders can analyze larger volumes of malware in less time, while attackers can misuse the same capability to considerably accelerate and scale vulnerability research and exploit development, shortening the time to exploitation and increasing the volume of intrusions.

As part of our broader innovation initiative for applying AI to automate and scale up defense workflows to keep up with an increasingly fast and widespread threat landscape, this work contributes to making LLM-driven reverse engineering inspectable, continuable, and reusable. These properties are important when reverse engineering output is used as part of cyber defense operations, such as incident response, detection development, or threat hunting, where analysts act on this output, share it with other stakeholders, and use it as input to other tools and workflows. This requires the ability to inspect the evidence behind an LLM's conclusions to verify them, have another analyst or model continue the work from where the LLM stopped, and reuse results coupled with the code and data they describe.

To this end, we focus on LLM-driven reverse engineering whose output is an annotated disassembler database, such as an IDA Pro, Ghidra, or Binary Ninja database. In contrast to a textual report, which reduces the analysis to a prose snapshot of the model's conclusions, detached from the code that supports them, an annotated database records findings directly on the disassembled code and data, as labels, types, data structures, and comments.

As a result, an analyst can verify each conclusion against the code and data it describes. When the database is shared with other stakeholders, recipients get every annotation, not only the findings a report would contain, and can verify and use the parts they need. In addition, another analyst or LLM can continue the analysis from the existing annotations in the database or correct them if necessary, rather than interpreting a prose report and locating the code and data each conclusion refers to. Other tools and workflows can also work directly with the findings and the code they apply to, for example, to generate YARA rules that target functions identified as implementing specific capabilities, or to parse configuration data using recovered data structures.

However, an annotated database provides these benefits only if its annotations are accurate and complete, which LLMs do not guarantee. To understand these limitations in practice, we conducted evaluation studies in which LLMs analyzed binaries and annotated IDA databases without safeguards for the accuracy or completeness of their work.

We first present the results of these studies, which show that models produced inaccurate labels, left some findings unrecorded, lost track of unfinished work, and stopped the analysis early. Full model specifics are provided in the section below.

Based on these findings, we propose a standard for LLM-driven reverse engineering that annotates disassembler databases. Under the standard, each annotation must be confirmed as recorded in the database and traceable to documented evidence against which its accuracy can be verified, outstanding work stays tracked until it is resolved, and an independent review assesses the accuracy of the annotations and identifies work left undone, returning its findings to the LLM that reverse engineers the binary for correction.

Finally, we present VerifiedIDA, a harness that serves as a preliminary implementation of the standard by mediating the LLM's access to an IDA database. VerifiedIDA is released as an open-source project, together with the specification of the standard and a user guide.

Evaluation Studies | LLM-Driven Reverse Engineering Without Safeguards

The goal of our evaluation studies was to identify common challenges with model-led reverse engineering where the model had to annotate a disassembler database using basic tooling. A detailed comparison of how models perform, individually or by vendor or tier, was not our focus.

We used proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI in addition to open-source models to reverse engineer binaries of varying size, both malicious and legitimate. The majority of our testing presented here used GPT-5.6 Sol. The models worked through a simple harness, in which an LLM analyzes a binary autonomously, without any human or automated feedback and with access only to basic reverse engineering capabilities. The harness provides only general instructions and a fixed set of tools for viewing disassembled and decompiled code, following cross-references, searching the binary, and writing labels, types, and comments, such as free-text descriptions of functions, into an IDA database.

The full reasoning of Anthropic and OpenAI models is not available through their APIs, so we could not directly observe how they make decisions while reverse engineering a binary. Instead, we logged each analysis step by step in what we refer to as an LLM log, recording the tools the model called, the code it retrieved, its intermediate notes and planned next steps, and the edits it made to the database. An LLM log may show, for example, the model retrieving the pseudocode of a function, following its cross-references, and then labeling the function in the database. This allowed us to reconstruct what the model retrieved, what it based each annotation on, and how it acted on that information.

To illustrate some of the observations we discuss next, we present two case studies in the Case Studies section, each examining in detail how GPT-5.6 Sol performed a routine reverse engineering task. In both, the model reverse engineered a sample of ComRAT (SHA-1 hash: 0139818441431c72a1935e7f740a1cc458a63452), a backdoor attributed to the Russian APT group Turla. Case Study #1 covers the recovery of a data structure passed as a parameter to two ComRAT functions, whereas Case Study #2 covers the analysis of a single ComRAT function's behavior.

Structured Work Grounded in Evidence

We observed that the LLMs took a sound, methodical approach to reverse engineering tasks. For example, when labeling a variable or a function, they typically started with a broad analysis of the pseudocode or disassembly and then moved to targeted exploration, analyzing how the variable or function is used across the binary to determine the variable’s role or the function’s primary operation, which is what the label should describe.

The models also largely avoided fabrication. For example, when a model could not establish the role or type of a variable, it typically applied a generic label, such as unknown, or a generic data type, such as void, rather than inventing one the code did not support.

In addition, the LLMs made effective use of authoritative information relevant to the analysis, such as the public documentation of Windows API functions, which is highly likely present in their training data. For example, when a variable was passed to a Windows API function, they typed it based on the function's documented parameter types, and when a function called Windows API functions, they took the documented behavior of these API functions into account when determining the primary operation of the calling function.

Inaccurate and Incomplete Disassembler Databases

Alongside the strengths discussed above, we observed four major, recurring problems. These problems undermine the purpose of an annotated database as the primary output of LLM-driven reverse engineering, which is to serve as an accurate and complete binary-grounded foundation for any downstream use.

Accuracy of labels

Some labels the LLMs applied to variables and functions did not accurately describe the variables' roles or the functions' primary operations. This matters because analysts often rely on labels to navigate an annotated disassembler database. Inaccurate labels therefore have consequences for anyone who uses an annotated disassembler database, human or model, whether to continue an analysis or to draw conclusions from it. For example, an ambiguous label may lead an analyst to redo work that is already done, while an imprecise one may draw attention away from binary behavior that matters.

Inaccurate labels also misrepresent the binary under analysis, and any conclusion drawn from the database carries that misrepresentation forward. In addition, the inaccuracy of a label is not apparent from the database itself, since a label says nothing about how well it is supported. An inaccurate label is therefore either taken at face value, with the consequences that may bring, or caught only at the cost of redoing the analysis whose conclusion it was meant to record.

Capture of findings

The models repeatedly established findings during the analysis without recording them as annotations in the databases, that is, they did not reliably translate reverse engineering findings into database annotations. These findings did not survive the analysis sessions, and the effort behind them was effectively lost, leaving the databases incomplete.

Continuity of work

As the analyses progressed, the models often lost track of unfinished work, which we suspect is primarily due to context compaction, the condensing of the models' earlier output and tool results to fit their context windows. Steps they had planned were dropped, leaving the parts of the binary they targeted unanalyzed and without annotations in the databases.

Completeness of analysis

The LLMs often stopped exploring before examining all the code relevant to what they were analyzing. For example, having settled on a function's primary operation, an LLM labeled the function without exploring all of the function's callees, some of which implement additional capabilities. These capabilities remained unidentified, and the function's label did not express them.

Reverse Engineering Standard

The four problems we observed are not variations of a single failure. Each points to a responsibility that cannot be left to the model alone.

Models are not infallible, so no system can guarantee that every label they apply is accurate. A system can, however, keep the evidence behind each annotation, so an inaccurate label can be found and corrected without redoing the analysis it was meant to record. It can confirm which findings reach the database, carry unfinished work beyond the model's context, and check whether the code behind a conclusion was examined.

These checks fall into two categories. Mechanical checks can be made without interpreting the code: whether a requested change persisted, or whether a function's callees were inspected before the function was labeled, as in Case Study #2. Semantic checks require review on whether a label describes a function's primary operation, or whether the analysis establishes how two capabilities relate.

This is the division of labor at the center of our standard: the model makes the analytical judgments, and the system around it preserves the evidence, maintains the state of the project, and enforces follow-through. We formalize this into four requirements.

Problem

Requirement

What the system must establish

Accuracy of labels

Attributable evidence

What each annotation is based on, so its accuracy can be verified

Capture of findings

Verified changes

What was requested, what was recorded, and whether it persisted

Continuity of work

Preserved project state

What is known, what has been done, and what is planned next

Completeness of analysis

Enforceable scope and review

What must be examined, and what remains unresolved

Attributable evidence. Every annotation must be traceable to the evidence the model retrieved to support it, identified by the binary and the state of the database it came from. Evidence that no longer reflects the current database must not support new annotations.

Verified changes. The system must check what each requested change recorded in the database and whether it persisted. If a change fails, the accepted database must stay intact, and the model must receive feedback it can act on. This matters most for type changes. A recovered structure that cannot be applied cleanly, or that alters parts of the database the model did not intend to change, can be detected and rejected mechanically before it affects how other code decompiles.

Preserved project state. Accepted annotations, the history of changes, the working summary of the binary, and the list of pending tasks must be stored outside the model's context. The analysis can then be resumed after context compaction, an interruption, or a switch to another binary, by the same model, a different one, or a human analyst.

Enforceable scope and review. An independent reviewer must be able to challenge the accuracy of annotations and identify work left undone. Its findings must go back to the investigating model and stay tracked until each is corrected, rejected with evidence, or recorded as unresolved for a human to pick up.

Our proposed standard is the floor for LLM-driven reverse engineering. It does not make a model's analysis correct, and it does not prescribe how a model should reverse engineer a binary. Many tools already use models for reverse engineering in their own ways, and more will follow. Verification is essential, but it establishes only what was recorded, not whether it is right, and review by another model or by an expert human can still miss errors. What the standard ensures is that the model's conclusions remain tied to evidence that can be revisited, and that its mistakes are identifiable rather than hidden. The standard is also independent of a particular disassembler. We publish it as an interface specification alongside our reference implementation for IDA Pro, which we describe next.

The VerifiedIDA Harness

VerifiedIDA is our reference implementation of the standard. We built it for IDA Pro first because it is the disassembler our team works with most. The model chooses what to investigate, inspects code, and proposes annotations. VerifiedIDA acts as the host and mediates every access to the IDA database: it identifies the target of each request, requires current evidence, applies edits to a candidate copy of the database, checks the result, and records each operation. It maintains three records:

IDA databases, which hold the accepted labels, comments, types, interfaces, and relationships, one per binary, including embedded binaries.

A SQLite ledger, which holds inspections, operations, verification results, database revisions, and tracked work.

A project notebook, which holds the model's current understanding, uncertainties, and next actions, along with a journal of how they changed.

Attributable evidence. Every edit must cite evidence the host recorded for the current target and database revision. Evidence is identified by binary and revision rather than by address alone, because a binary and the binaries embedded in it can use the same addresses. If the database has changed since the model inspected the code, the host rejects the edit and explains how to obtain current evidence. Model inferences and historical evidence are labeled as such. A reviewer can start from any annotation, find the operation that introduced it in the ledger, and examine the code the model was shown when it made it.

Verified changes. The host applies each edit to an isolated candidate database, reads the result back through a separate path, and checks it before the candidate becomes the accepted database. Type and prototype edits also receive a comparison of the affected IDA state, and unrelated changes lead to rejection. If an edit fails, the accepted database is left unchanged, and the model receives the target, the failed stage, the requested and observed state, and a recovery direction. Checkpoints reopen the database in a fresh IDA process to confirm that accepted changes persisted.

Feedback also targets the capture problem directly. After an edit, the host flags incomplete annotations, such as a renamed function without a behavior comment or parameters that retain generated names, and reports where a newly created type is not yet applied. In our worked example, based on the ComRAT structure from Case Study #1, the feedback reported that the structure the model had created was declared but not used anywhere, and the model went on to apply it to the function's parameter.

Preserved project state. The notebook records where the investigation stands, and its current-state sections are rewritten as the model's understanding changes. After context compaction, the model is given its current instructions and the recorded project state, and any further edit still requires fresh evidence from IDA. When the model follows an embedded binary, the host records the child's bytes, how it was extracted, and its link to the parent, and opens a separate database for it. Before switching, we require the model to record what it has established in the parent and how the parent uses the child, so it knows where to return.

Enforceable scope and review. Independent review starts with the host building an inventory of annotations and possible gaps. Reviewer models then examine individual claims and the overall explanation of the program, with read-only access to disposable copies of the databases. The host validates their findings and freezes the scope of required corrections. The investigating model then resumes and works through one finding at a time: it can apply the correction, revise it, reject it with evidence, defer it, or request a specific follow-up. It then checks that the accepted review conclusions agree with the annotations, and any remaining disagreement blocks completion. The final report states what was verified, what remains unresolved, and whether the completion policy was met.

Coverage mode. We reran the Case Study #2 function with an experimental call-flow mode enabled. In six earlier GPT-5.6 Sol runs, none had opened sub_180081450, and the four that annotated the parent all omitted forwarded-export handling.

In the new run, Sol began from a clean database and was not told which callee mattered. Once it committed a claim about sub_180077C10, the mode listed the function's 20 direct internal callees and held that claim open until each had a recorded outcome. Sol opened sub_180081450, identified it as the recursive resolver for forwarded exports, and confirmed a parent comment that separates local export-table parsing from the recursion it delegates.

A repeat under a revised policy reached the same result across all 20 callees, and every edit survived a fresh-process reload. The mode follows direct calls only. An early attempt to apply it across the whole project generated 265 required nodes for eight edits, so we reserve it for selected claims.

Conclusion

Over the past year we’ve watched the infosec community grapple with the rapid adoption of AI tools and increased automation. It is clear that AI models can now reverse engineer binaries at a scale no team of analysts can match. As the volume of analysis the models produce grows, it creates a widening gap in our ability to understand how decisions were reached and what evidence they were based on. After all, a model's labels, types, and descriptions are only as useful as an analyst's ability to confirm them, correct them, and build on them.

A database makes this level of inspection possible in a way that a report cannot because each conclusion can be tied to the code it describes. This allows a person (or another model) to easily continue the work or incorporate the findings into downstream detection and hunting workflows.

LLMs give us the opportunity to automate more security analysis but only insofar as the work they produce remains understandable. Scaling the analysis without also scaling our ability to inspect it replaces one bottleneck with another.

Our evaluation studies showed that models alone do not reliably produce attestable databases. Labels drift from what the code does, findings stay in logs, planned work disappears, and analysis stops before the relevant code has been read. The standard and VerifiedIDA respond by leaving the analytical judgment with the model and giving the system around it the job of keeping that judgment checkable. Our rerun of Case Study #2 shows the difference: the helper that six earlier runs skipped became work the model could not leave unfinished.

We are releasing both as a starting point. The requirements describe the minimum a model-driven workflow should provide, and our implementation covers a single disassembler. We invite the community to test the specification against their own tooling, build adapters for Ghidra and Binary Ninja, and push back on requirements that do not hold up. Where sharing is permitted, we also encourage researchers to publish annotated projects alongside their reports, so others can extend an analysis instead of repeating it.

This paper complements research we presented at LABScon 2026.

Case Studies

#1 | Recovering a Data Structure

Recovering data structures is routine reverse engineering work. At the memory level, a structure is a base address with fields at fixed offsets from it, where a field may be a complex data type itself. If the binary carries no debug symbols, it does not declare field offsets, types, and names, and these have to be recovered through analysis.

Two ComRAT functions, with the IDA default names sub_18002C770 and sub_18002CDA0, receive a pointer to a data structure as their parameter. IDA types these parameters as an integer.

The LLM typed the parameters as a pointer to a data structure, which it declared as follows.

The LLM approached the recovery of the structure in two stages. First, from the pseudocode of sub_18002C770, sub_18002CDA0, and the functions they invoke, it observed references to specific offsets from the function parameter value (the structure base address), concluding that the parameter is a pointer to a structure. It then widened the analysis to the rest of ComRAT's code, looking for references to the structure's fields wherever they occur. For each field it identified, it analyzed the context in which the field is used to propose a label, type, and size.

This enabled the LLM to recover the full set of structure fields, and from their sizes the correct total size of the structure itself.

The strongest evidence the LLM had for typing a field was its use as a parameter to a Windows API function. Many Windows API functions are documented publicly and their parameter sets are relatively stable, so the types of these parameters are highly likely present in the model's training data. IDA may also expose these types in the pseudocode provided to the LLM since it auto-defines parameter types for many of these functions. The model could therefore determine field types from authoritative sources.

For example, the LLM observed that a pointer to the structure field at offset 0x30 is passed as the tenth parameter of CreateProcessW. Microsoft documents the type of this parameter as a pointer to a PROCESS_INFORMATION structure, and IDA's pseudocode shows the same type. The LLM used this information to correctly type the field as PROCESS_INFORMATION.

The LLM did not produce annotations that its analysis did not support. For example, it found no use of the field at offset 0x28 within the functions under analysis and did not label the field after an invented role. Instead, it flagged the finding and decided to explore ComRAT's code further to establish the field's role. It found no use of the field anywhere in ComRAT and labeled it unresolved_28. Our own analysis confirms that the field is indeed never used.

However, several structure field and function labels produced by the LLM are inaccurate, since they do not describe what they should: the role a field plays in the code or the primary operation a function performs. For example, the LLM labeled the field at offset 0x28 unresolved_28, naming its own analytical state rather than the role of the field, or the lack thereof. The label is also ambiguous, because it does not distinguish a field that has not been examined from one that has been examined and found to be unused. In the case of this field, a name such as unused would be more appropriate.

The LLM also named the function sub_18002C770 PrepareSuspendedSurrogateProcess, although the function’s primary operation is the creation of a browser process in a suspended state. The LLM’s label does not indicate process creation at all, and Prepare suggests work that precedes a later step rather than the function’s primary operation. The LLM’s free-text description of the function (“Create the configured surrogate process before proxy injection”) shows that the model had identified the primary operation. The description leads with it and treats the injection that follows as context, whereas the label PrepareSuspendedSurrogateProcess keeps only the context and leaves out the process creation. A human reverse engineer would be more likely to apply a label such as CreateSuspendedBrowserProcess, which is more descriptive and more accurate in the context of the task.

Beyond inaccurate labels, the LLM did not record all of its findings in the IDA database, as the annotation of the structure field at offset 0x0 demonstrates. This field is a pointer to a structure, which holds data associated with a log writing mechanism, and the LLM logs show that the model identified the field as such.

However, in the IDA database, the LLM typed this field as a generic void pointer and labeled it owner_context rather than something closer to its role, such as LogWriter. The LLM had established the type and role of the field but did not translate these findings into IDA database annotations.

#2 | Analyzing a Function’s Behavior

A ComRAT function, with the IDA default name sub_180077C10, retrieves by name the address of a function exported by a dynamic link library (DLL) loaded in a remote process. If the export is forwarded to another DLL, the function resolves the address of the forwarded export recursively.

The LLM labeled this function ResolveRemoteExportAddress, correctly expressing its primary operation. As in Case Study #1, the strongest evidence the LLM relied on was the Windows API calls the function invokes. ResolveRemoteExportAddress also compares values against publicly documented constants, which provided the LLM with further authoritative evidence of the function’s operation.

For example, from the ReadProcessMemory calls, the LLM established that the function reads memory in the address space of a remote process. From the comparisons against the MZ (0x5A4D) and PE (0x4550) signature constants, the model determined that the function looks for Windows PE (Portable Executable) headers. Because the PE format is publicly documented and highly likely present in the model’s training data, the offsets into these headers visible in the pseudocode enabled the model to identify which of the DLL’s PE structures the function reads, such as its export directory and the array of names of its exported functions.

The LLM's free-text description, “Resolve an exported function address in a remote module from its PE export directory”, is accurate but incomplete, since it does not account for the resolution of forwarded exports.

If an export is forwarded to another DLL, sub_180077C10 (ResolveRemoteExportAddress) calls sub_180081450, which resolves the address of the forwarded export. Treating its understanding of sub_180077C10 as complete, the LLM labeled and described the function without exploring all of its callees, including sub_180081450. The capability implemented by sub_180081450 therefore remained unidentified.

articles.title: Defrost and Disrupt | An Assessment of Europe’s Refrigeration Attacks
articles.context: The incidents came three weeks after attacks on refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

On November 2 and 3, supermarket chains in Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia reported overnight disruption to store refrigeration systems. The incidents came three weeks after attacks on refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets.

Attacks on refrigeration systems predate the 2026 incidents, including attacks on Russian supermarkets and Israeli stores documented by Danfoss in 2022, and a 2024 attack on a Los Angeles meat processor that the DOJ attributed to CARR.

Reporting and official statements suggest attackers changed temperature and defrost settings through the systems’ own management interfaces. ANSSI’s assessment of the French cases at the time pointed to internet-exposed administration interfaces and weak passwords.

Russian-aligned groups including CARR, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest have a documented record of disrupting operational technology and have claimed refrigeration intrusions, making them a credible line of investigation. However, available evidence does not yet establish who is responsible for the European incidents.

Freezer failures at U.S. military commissaries in August predate the French attacks. U.S. officials reportedly suspect Iran-linked actors in those cases, an assessment that is provisional and does not concern Europe.

Further incidents are likely wherever the same access conditions persist. Copied techniques and opportunistic claims may make unrelated activity look like a single campaign before investigators establish whether one exists.

Overview and Chronology

Reporting on the recent spate of incidents affecting store refrigeration systems in Europe has moved quickly, at times conflating them with older attacks, hacktivist claims and government allegations about Russian and Iranian actors. The chronology below separates incidents from claims and from assessments. When reviewed in order, it shows similar incidents recurring across countries and months but does not establish that these various incidents belong to a single campaign.

2022 - Danfoss documented attacks targeting 16 Russian supermarkets and affecting 40 Israeli stores. According to the vendor, the affected Israeli installations lacked appropriate firewall or VPN protection.

November 2024 - A Los Angeles meat-processing facility suffered an attack that, according to later U.S. Justice Department allegations, spoiled meat and caused an ammonia leak. The DOJ attributed that incident to CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn, or CARR.

December 9, 2025 - The DOJ announced allegations of Russian government backing for CARR and NoName057(16). A concurrent multinational advisory documented associated groups’ opportunistic attacks against operational technology.

Late August–September 1, 2026 - Refrigeration failures affected at least six U.S. military commissaries, the grocery stores serving military personnel. By September 1, Stars and Stripes had reported that three military criminal-investigation agencies were investigating. Their involvement was therefore public well before October’s reporting about suspected hacking.

October 11–13, 2026 - Hundreds of French supermarkets experienced refrigeration disruption. The Paris prosecutor’s cybercrime section opened an investigation the same day, and on October 13 Economy Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament that approximately 700 stores had been affected. CERT-FR issued its alert on October 12 and expanded the affected-equipment list on October 13. It encompasses Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC equipment alongside Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems.

October 21, 2026 - ANSSI director Vincent Strubel told the French Senate that the agency’s assessment at the time pointed to exposed administration and weak passwords, rather than the previously publicized vulnerabilities discussed in early coverage.

October 29, 2026 - Reuters reported, citing four officials, that the Pentagon was treating the August commissary failures as suspected hacking. Separately, Nextgov/FCW reported that officials suspected Iran-linked actors, citing two people familiar with the matter. The Iran assessment was provisional and concerned the U.S. cases, not the European incidents.

November 2-3, 2026 - Further refrigeration incidents were reported in Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden. In Finland, Kesko also reported temperature anomalies at a few smaller stores and said it was investigating the cause, without ruling out interference over the network.

The German reporting illustrates the distinction between incident dates and disclosure dates. WDR reported affected stores in North Rhine-Westphalia on November 2, while BR’s November 3 report described manipulation at an Edeka store in Reisbach overnight into November 2.

Our chronology shows that refrigeration attacks predate the current wave. Danfoss documented attacks on Russian and Israeli stores in 2022, and the DOJ attributed the 2024 Los Angeles meat-processing incident to CARR.

The U.S. commissary failures came before the French attacks. Reuters reported on October 29 that the Pentagon was treating those failures as suspected hacking and that U.S. and French investigators were coordinating, although that does not establish a common perpetrator. By that time, the outages were two months old, and military investigators’ involvement had been public since September 1.

Further, while Russian-linked activity and the Iran suspicion appear in the same chronology because both are part of the public record on these incidents, they concern different actors and different incident clusters. The Russian-linked entries are precedent from 2024 and 2025, and the Iran suspicion relates only to the U.S. commissary cases.

Suspected Attack Method

These incidents involve commercial supervisory platforms that centralize management of refrigeration equipment across a site, letting operators monitor equipment, adjust settings, review alarms and perform maintenance remotely. An attacker who gains control-capable access to the management interface can change operational settings and push refrigeration outside its intended conditions.

How attackers reached those interfaces is a separate question; however, early coverage focused on published vulnerabilities in Danfoss controllers, including authentication-bypass and command-injection flaws documented in Claroty’s research. On October 21, ANSSI director Vincent Strubel told a French Senate hearing that, according to the agency’s assessment at the time, those vulnerabilities were not the ones exploited, pointing instead to exposed administration and weak passwords.

ANSSI’s assessment covers the French cases, and it is not yet known whether the same access path applies to the November 2-3 incidents or the U.S. commissaries. The documented vulnerabilities remain a risk for any operator running unpatched or end-of-life controllers.

Attribution

Responsibility for the European incidents has not been publicly established. Russian-aligned disruptive actors are one credible hypothesis, based on precedent shown in the chronology, including the DOJ’s allegations about CARR and NoName057(16) and its attribution of the 2024 Los Angeles incident to CARR.

Notably, SentinelLABS has previously documented how NoName057(16) organizes and publicizes its DDoS operations against Ukraine and NATO countries.

The multinational advisory published alongside the DOJ’s allegations assessed that CARR administrators and a NoName057(16) administrator went on to form Z-Pentest after dissatisfaction with GRU support, and that Z-Pentest operates separately from GRU involvement.

DOJ’s December 9 announcement, summarizing the indictments, instead describes CARR as “also known as Z-Pentest.” These public descriptions do not fully resolve the relationship between the groups or the extent of state direction over particular operations. Neither establishes responsibility for the current refrigeration incidents.

Z-Pentest has since claimed a refrigeration intrusion. An archived Telegram repost attributed to the group describes a purported joint operation with NoName057(16) against refrigeration controls at a Spanish supermarket, claiming access that would allow changes to temperatures and equipment operation. The repost survives in a third-party archive and confirms neither access nor damage, nor any link to the current attacks.

Independent ideological operators, copycats, financially motivated intruders and other state-linked actors also fit the public facts, as does Iran-linked involvement in the U.S. cases, where officials’ suspicion remains unverified.

Moving past these hypotheses would require evidence tying affected environments to an operator, such as access records, infrastructure with meaningful provenance, distinctive sequences of configuration changes, validated account activity, or actor material containing verifiable details that weren’t already public. A familiar target, a shared controller model or a similar temperature change would not be enough, because there are only a limited number of obvious ways to disrupt the same equipment.

Investigators may hold evidence of this kind that has not been released. Without it, outside observers cannot yet independently substantiate a specific attribution.

Targeting and Motivation

Under a Russian-aligned scenario, these attacks could serve both disruptive and influence objectives. Visible interference with familiar civilian services can impose costs in countries supporting Ukraine and convey that ordinary services remain within reach, a message that requires no threat to the food supply itself.

Individual targets may also have been chosen for a simpler reason, which is that the systems were accessible. The joint advisory describes pro-Russia groups as selecting victims on superficial criteria such as availability and existing vulnerabilities, so a disruption with strategic value need not involve a strategically chosen target.

The “hacktivist” label describes how such groups present themselves and is not a reliable guide to their capability, independence or potential for harm.

Nonetheless, ambiguity of motivation is sometimes an objective. Beyond undermining domestic faith in governments, this is a relatively low resource intrusion that can produce expensive, irreversible consequences to everyday people.

Outlook

Further attempts are likely wherever the same access conditions persist. Industry and government organizations have warned that the cheap, repeatable techniques used by pro-Russian groups can be adopted by others, and the suspected method needs little beyond access, so continued activity could involve previous operators, unrelated groups or both.

New victims and opportunistic claims can make unrelated activity look like a single campaign before investigators establish whether one exists. Similar outcomes already have more than one suspected actor, with Russian-aligned groups a credible hypothesis for the European cases and Iran-linked actors provisionally suspected in the U.S. cases.

Shared maintenance access deserves scrutiny. Portugal’s Mosqueteiros group said incidents at seven Intermarché stores appeared to target an external provider responsible for refrigeration management. In Germany, an operator also described an attack involving its refrigeration-maintenance company. These accounts make third-party access an important investigative lead, but do not establish one compromised provider, a common intrusion path across countries, or a compromised software-update channel.

Portugal’s Mosqueteiros group said the incidents at seven Intermarché stores appeared to involve an external provider responsible for refrigeration management. In Germany, an AWO representative also described an attack involving the company remotely maintaining an affected store’s refrigeration. These operator accounts make third-party access an important investigative lead, but do not establish one compromised provider, a common intrusion path across countries, or a compromised software-update channel. Investigators should examine whether accounts, gateways or administrative infrastructure connect multiple affected locations.

Mitigation Guidance

Where safely practicable, preserve relevant logs and configuration records before restarting or resetting equipment. Coordinate recovery with refrigeration personnel, prioritizing physical safety and safe operating conditions.CERT-FR’s alert on the French incidents sets out steps for operators of the affected Danfoss, Copeland and Dixell equipment. It calls for removing those units, and any other equipment on a public IP address, from internet exposure, checking insurance terms first if doing so cuts the data feed to the refrigeration contractor, and reviewing the complete configuration, defrost ranges in particular. It advises restoring access only through a secure VPN or protected network, with firewall filtering of contractors’ source addresses acceptable only as a stopgap, and applying the manufacturer’s hardening guidance, such as firmware updates and changed default passwords.

For compromised units, it advises a restart or factory reset followed by reconfiguration, and it warns that a reset alone will not prevent re-compromise of an end-of-life device that stays exposed.

The December 2025 joint advisory from the FBI, CISA, NSA and international partners addresses its mitigations to OT owners and operators generally. It recommends scanning owned IP ranges for exposed systems, including connections set up by third parties, segmenting IT from OT networks, using MFA where possible and strong, unique passwords where it is not, and limiting remotely accessible accounts to view-only. It also recommends reviewing setpoint ranges with alerting for deviations, keeping backups of controller configurations, and practicing manual operation.

For exposed systems with weak or default credentials, the advisory says to assume compromise. Its response steps include isolating affected hosts, scoping the intrusion by reviewing unusual authentications and recent network connections, issuing new credentials and reporting the compromise to the relevant authorities.

Conclusion

Attacks on retail and food-industry refrigeration predate the 2026 incidents, with Danfoss documenting cases at Russian and Israeli stores in 2022 and the DOJ attributing a 2024 attack on a Los Angeles meat processor to CARR.

In the French cases, ANSSI’s assessment at the time pointed to exposed management interfaces and weak passwords, conditions that guidance from CERT-FR and the joint advisory addresses directly.

The public record does not yet establish who was responsible for the European incidents or whether they form a single campaign. Further incidents are likely wherever the same access conditions remain.

articles.title: Stop Chasing CVEs: Start Governing Software Dependencies
articles.context: Sonatype's analysis of 1,552 open source CVEs found that 64% had no CVSS score, severity categories matched across sources only 19% of the time, and scoring delays averaged six...
articles.full_text:
A new vulnerability disclosure can set off a familiar chain of work. You check whether or not an application uses the affected component, determine whether the vulnerable code is reachable, find a fixed version, test the upgrade, and get it into production. Then the next advisory arrives.

Known vulnerabilities need to be understood and remediated. But a process built around chasing CVEs one at a time can leave teams reacting to risk after a dependency has already entered their software.

It also leaves important questions unanswered:

Is the package malicious?

Is its license acceptable?

Is the project still maintained?

Can its origin be verified?

Does the dependency meet the organization's requirements?

A CVE is a useful signal, but it is not a complete measure of component trust. Teams need to govern the software dependencies they use across the SDLC, from selection and approval through ongoing monitoring and remediation.

CVE Remediation Is Necessary. It Is Not the Whole Strategy.

The CVE system gives security teams, developers, vendors, and researchers a shared way to identify known vulnerabilities. But a CVE record or score does not show whether vulnerable code is reachable in an application, whether a dependency is direct or transitive, or whether a safe upgrade is available.

Sonatype's analysis of 1,552 open source CVEs found that 64% had no CVSS score, severity categories matched across sources only 19% of the time, and scoring delays averaged six weeks. Those gaps can make it difficult to rank findings and decide where engineering time will reduce the most risk.

Teams need to treat CVEs as one input and weigh them alongside component use, available fixes, and application context.

Disclosure Starts the Remediation Cycle

When vulnerability management centers on incoming CVEs, teams begin responding after disclosure: identifying affected versions, tracing dependencies, and coordinating upgrades. By then, a component may already appear across applications, build environments, and releases, adding to the remediation backlog.

Component risks also extend beyond CVEs. A package may be malicious, poorly maintained, or incompatible with licensing requirements. Finding those issues earlier can help teams avoid broader changes, release delays, and retesting.

AI Is Increasing the Pace of Discovery and Consumption

AI is changing how quickly teams find and use software components. A developer might ask a coding assistant to add a feature, accept its suggestion to use a new library, and move on to the next task. The package can become part of the project before anyone has checked whether it is maintained, allowed by policy, or appropriate for that use. Consequently, teams must absorb a higher volume of vulnerability disclosures while simultaneously tracking which components enter their codebase and why.

A large Spring security disclosure illustrates the downstream scale. In August 2026, Sonatype tracked 91 CVEs across Spring and related projects. At the time of publication, Sonatype Guide reported 148,608 affected components, including components that bundle vulnerable Spring code. The disclosure does not establish that AI caused those vulnerabilities, but it shows how broadly a vulnerability can affect software that depends on an ecosystem.

Teams responding to disclosures at this scale need to determine:

Which applications include the affected components, directly or transitively?

Which vulnerable versions are present or deployed?

Which components pose the greatest risk in their environment?

Which upgrades will address the vulnerabilities without causing unnecessary disruption?

Discovery can move faster than downstream teams can locate, assess, and upgrade affected components. As AI-assisted vulnerability research develops, vulnerability intelligence and remediation processes will need to keep pace.

Teams also need visibility into what is in their software, where it came from, how it is used, and who owns decisions to keep, upgrade, replace, or accept it. That context helps turn a stream of findings into work that can be prioritized and acted on.

Component Risk Goes Beyond Vulnerabilities

A component can create risk even when it has no known CVE. A more complete assessment considers several dimensions:

Malware: Has the package or release been compromised, or does it contain malicious behavior?

Licensing: Is its license compatible with the project's obligations and intended use?

Maintenance: Is the project maintained, and can the team rely on its release and support practices?

Provenance: Can the component's source and history be verified?

Policy: Does it meet the organization's requirements for approved sources, versions, and use cases?

Each scenario demands distinct evidence and action: fixing vulnerable releases, instantly blocking malicious packages, scheduling replacements for unmaintained libraries, legally reviewing licenses, or verifying provenance prior to approval.

Treating every issue as another scanner finding can obscure those differences. Component governance gives teams a way to define which qualities matter, set expectations before adoption, and assign an appropriate response when a component falls outside them.

Govern Dependencies Before and After Adoption

Governance works best when it is part of normal development, rather than a review that begins after a release is ready.

Teams can make it practical by connecting policy to the component lifecycle:

Define acceptable use. Establish requirements for sources, licenses, maintenance, provenance, and known security risks. Set policies that reflect how components will be used and the impact of a failure.

Evaluate before adoption. Check candidate components against those requirements before they become dependencies. Give developers and AI tools clear, approved choices where possible, so the compliant path is also the easy path.

Maintain a record of use. Track component identity and version, origin, dependency relationships, and the applications or releases that include it. This context helps teams understand the reach of a new advisory or policy change.

Monitor for change. A component's status can change after adoption. New vulnerability information may emerge; a project may become inactive; a release may be compromised; or an organization's policy may change. Reassess components as new evidence arrives.

Route decisions to owners. Define who handles upgrades, replacement, license review, and exceptions. Record the reason for an exception and when it should be reviewed again.

Scanning and patching remain essential, but connecting them to a broader decision framework lets teams weigh vulnerabilities against exposure, exploitability, available fixes, and business context. Meanwhile, malware alerts, licensing issues, and maintenance risks can be routed directly to the appropriate decision-makers.

Effective open source policy enforcement aligns with risk severity. Known malware warrants immediate blocking, licensing queries require review before distribution, and unmaintained low-risk components may receive temporary exceptions. Explicit thresholds, designated owners, and time-bound exceptions enable consistent standard application without unnecessary escalations or blanket bans.

Timing is critical. Providing developers and AI tools with trusted, policy-approved component options during dependency selection allows teams to address risk before it is built in. Identifying flagged components later in release pipelines forces teams to reverse decisions already embedded across repositories and applications.

Move From a Findings Queue to Better Decisions

Software teams will continue to receive CVEs, and they should continue to remediate vulnerabilities that put their applications at risk. But a growing list of CVEs is not, by itself, a strategy for choosing and managing software components.

A stronger approach starts earlier and continues after adoption. It helps teams select components that meet their needs, understand where those components are used, detect changes in their risk, and respond according to clear policies. That can reduce avoidable surprises and help engineering teams spend less time reconstructing dependency context during an incident.

The goal is not to eliminate vulnerability work. It is to make that work part of a more complete way to govern software components — one that accounts for security, licensing, maintenance, provenance, and policy throughout the software lifecycle.

Sonatype Nexus One platform helps put that strategy into practice and gives teams the data to assess open source dependencies. With trusted component intelligence and policies built into development workflows, teams can make better decisions about what they use and respond more effectively when the evidence changes. articles.context: Public proof-of-concept exploits allow local attackers to execute arbitrary code with root permissions on major Linux distributions running kernels released before May 13, 2026
articles.full_text:
The Good | Global Response Continues for PHP2SHELL Exploit Attempts & Defenders Dismantle Global Cybercrime Rings

This past week, cyber defenders responded to a cluster of vulnerability disclosures and security incidents collectively dubbed “Black October,” spanning flaws in PHP2SHELL, Node.js, GitLab, and Brotli, a software supply chain attack in LiteLLM, and compromised certificate authority keys at eMudhra.

Despite PHP2SHELL affecting roughly 70% of websites worldwide, mass, internet-wide exploitation of the kind seen with Log4SHELL hasn’t materialized. PHP2SHELL lacks a universal offset, since heap layouts, memory alignments, and worker states differ by PHP version, build, and SAPI configuration, and attackers must craft specific request streams to line up memory blocks before triggering the underlying out-of-memory error.

That complexity hasn’t stopped targeted compromises against systems, but it has kept broad, automated attacks from succeeding at scale. CISA added both PHP2SHELL CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, with a remediation deadline of October 29 for federal agencies.

International law enforcement this week also delivered major blows against cybercrime syndicates. Authorities extradited Chinese national Zheng Zhao from the Netherlands to California over an alleged multimillion-dollar cryptocurrency investment scheme that defrauded 174 American victims through fake trading platforms.

A U.S. federal court sentenced Ukrainian national Artem Stryzhak to 70 months in prison for conspiring to deploy Nefilim and Hive ransomware against hospitals, law firms, and other targets.

Finally, an international law enforcement coalition seized the domain of Virtualine, a “bulletproof” hosting provider that marketed itself to criminals for “all illegal/black hat activities”. Court records tie the seizure to Virtualine hosting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and non-consensual intimate imagery despite repeated takedown notices, plus money laundering that concealed the proceeds. Virtualine had also offered to quietly migrate a customer’s infrastructure to a shell company after law enforcement made contact.

The Bad | Threat Actors Chain Fragnesia Linux Flaw with PHP2SHELL to Root PAN-OS Firewalls

As part of Black October, researchers are warning that a high-severity Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw is being actively chained with the PHP2SHELL vulnerabilities. Tracked as CVE-2026-46300 and dubbed “Fragnesia,” the flaw stems from a logic defect in the Linux XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem that leaves stale page-cache writes exploitable for root access. Public proof-of-concept exploits allow local attackers to execute arbitrary code with root permissions on major Linux distributions running kernels released before May 13, 2026.

In response to active in-the-wild exploitation, CISA added Fragnesia to the KEV Catalog and mandated federal agencies patch affected systems under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, noting that threat actors are pairing it with the PHP2SHELL RCE flaws: exploiting PHP2SHELL first to implant a web shell, then using Fragnesia to escalate from that shell to full root control.

Security researchers uncovered a complete attack operation featuring custom weaponized exploit chains, target lists, detailed activity logs, and roughly 40 custom post-exploitation scripts. The campaign successfully rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers, whose web interface runs on PHP, across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including three systems in a U.S. government-affiliated environment.

Chaining an unauthenticated web flaw with a local kernel privilege escalation means patching either one alone isn’t enough. Closing the web shell’s entry point still leaves the root escalation path open on any system running a vulnerable kernel.

The Ugly | Silent Fix for Brotli Decoder Exposes Node2Shell Vulnerability

Security researchers uncovered a critical memory corruption vulnerability in the open-source Brotli compression decoder used across much of the web. Tracked as CVE-2026-111497 with a CVSS score of 9.2, the flaw, variously named Node2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Broccoli2Shell by the researchers who worked on it, stems from an out-of-bounds write when handling invalid stream block switches during decompression. It affects Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0, reaching major language runtimes and web frameworks including Node.js, Python, and .NET.

The flaw’s timeline stretches back further than its public disclosure. Upstream developers quietly fixed the underlying code on February 27 without a security advisory or CVE, and the vulnerability wasn’t publicly identified until a researcher team reported it in October.

Coordinated disclosure landed October 21, and fixes followed in waves: Python’s package registry shipped updates October 22 and 23, a Ruby gem update followed October 24, and .NET received an out-of-band patch on October 25, the same day researchers demonstrated working code execution on x86-64 against Node.js. Separate research into FFmpeg the same day produced a reproducible crash rather than confirmed code execution. Edge and hosting providers rolled out interim firewall mitigations within hours of the initial disclosure.

CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its KEV catalog on October 27, requiring federal remediation by November 10. Because proxy-level filtering doesn’t protect outbound client requests or file-based attack paths, closing this gap means upgrading the underlying Brotli library and rebuilding affected applications, not just patching at the network edge.

articles.title: Stopping Node2Shell: How SentinelOne Protects Customers From Brotli-Based Remote Code Execution

articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates that fix CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled with the runtime. Vendors have labeled the vulnerability Node2Shell, Brotli2Shell, Broccoli2Shell, and HTTP2Shell, because the flaw sits in Google's Brotli library and reaches software well beyond Node.js. Any application that decompresses attacker-controlled data with a vulnerable Brotli library could be at risk. Google, as the CVE Numbering Authority, scored it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, and Node.js rates it high.

CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 27, 2026, with a November 10, 2026 deadline for federal civilian agencies. The public telemetry we reviewed shows exploitation attempts against honeypot sensors, and researchers have demonstrated code execution in lab environments. As of October 29, 2026, we are not aware of a public report of a confirmed compromise of a production system.

This report details Node2Shell's mechanism, affected versions, and observed activity, and outlines how SentinelOne customers and partners can strengthen their defenses.

Key Highlights

One flaw, many patches. Node.js, Google Brotli, Bun, .NET, Python, Envoy, Istio, and PHP for Windows each shipped their own fix. Updating one does not update the others.

Attempts are confirmed. Production compromise is not. ELLIO and Previdian have each recorded an exploitation attempt against their honeypot sensors. Previdian notes that such observations do not show the target was vulnerable or that the attempt succeeded.

A default Node.js server is not exposed by itself. Something must hand attacker-controlled Brotli data to the decoder. Node.js names direct node:zlib use. Express 5 request bodies and built-in fetch() responses reach the same decoder, and Imperva reproduced both in the lab.

A failed exploit still costs you. The Node.js advisory lists a crash as an outcome, and Sysdig reports that crashes have been easy to reproduce. Repeated crashes are a denial of service against any service that decodes attacker-influenced Brotli.

The fix was visible for nearly eight months before release. Google committed it on February 27, 2026, with no release and no advisory. End-of-life Node.js 20, 23, and 25 are not expected to receive a fix.

Organizations should take the following steps immediately:

Upgrade Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, then restart processes and rebuild container images.

Inventory every other runtime and library that embeds the Brotli decoder, and patch internet-facing services first.

Where patching must wait, reject inbound requests that carry Content-Encoding: br at the proxy or load balancer.

What is Node2Shell

Node2Shell is a memory corruption flaw in the Brotli decoder, the code that expands Brotli-compressed data. A Brotli stream signals switches between block types. When a stream declares only one block type, a switch is invalid and the decoder should reject it. The vulnerable decoder instead reported the invalid switch as a request for more input. The caller supplied more bytes, and the decoder kept appending them to an eight-byte internal buffer and wrote past its end, according to the Node.js advisory.

Node.js lists the outcomes as a crash, disclosure of process memory, or remote code execution, and the CVE record describes the attacker as unauthenticated. Imperva demonstrated code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 arm64 image. Microsoft describes the .NET impact as information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

Routes that use express.json(), express.urlencoded(), express.text(), or express.raw() in Express 5 or body-parser 2 decompress bodies sent with Content-Encoding: br by default. Any client can send one.

Built-in fetch() decodes Brotli automatically, so a malicious or compromised server can target the client.

Applications that pass untrusted input to zlib.brotliDecompress() or zlib.createBrotliDecompress().

Recommended Mitigations

Patch, Restart, and Rebuild

Upgrade to a fixed Node.js release, update every Dockerfile that pins an older tag, and restart or redeploy every workload.

Confirm patch status from the Node.js release version running in each workload, not a bundled library version string, which may not reflect a backported fix.

Find Every Copy of the Decoder

Inventory Bun, .NET, Python Brotli, Envoy, Istio, PHP for Windows, and statically built executables, including staging, CI, build images, and developer machines.

Where Node.js links the system Brotli library, as it does on Debian, check your distribution’s advisory for the Node.js package as well as brotli. Debian’s tracker lists both.

PHP for Windows fixed the flaw with rebuilt packages that keep the same PHP version number, so php -v looks the same before and after. Check the -1 build suffix or the SHA-256 on the download page.

Move off Node.js 20, 23, and 25 on a defined date.

Reduce Exposure Until Patching Finishes

Reject requests with Content-Encoding: br at the WAF or proxy, or set the body-parser inflate option to false so compressed bodies return HTTP 415. The second option also rejects gzip and deflate bodies, so test client traffic first.

Restrict server-side fetches to trusted destinations. Link previews, webhooks, and crawlers send attacker-influenced URLs into fetch(), and removing br from Accept-Encoding does not stop a hostile server from replying with Brotli.

Enable a vendor WAF rule as a stopgap where one exists. It does not replace the upgrade.

Limit the Blast Radius

Run Node.js services as a non-root user and limit outbound connections from Node.js hosts. Docker runs containers as root by default, and the official node image provides a node user (uid 1000) that you must select with USER or -u.

Watch for Failed Attempts

Alert on repeated worker crashes after requests with Content-Encoding: br. Where core dumps are enabled, restrict who can read them and shorten retention, because a core file can hold memory contents from other users’ sessions.

How SentinelOne Protects You

Node2Shell exploits the Brotli decoder inside the Node.js process. Patching Node.js and every other copy of the Brotli decoder remains the primary control. SentinelOne provides detection and visibility into post-exploitation behavior while that work is underway.

The Singularity agent builds a storyline of process activity on a host, including the Node.js services targeted by Node2Shell. These processes have a predictable life: they answer requests, call APIs, and read files. They do not normally start /bin/sh, run reconnaissance commands, download executables into /tmp, or open connections to arbitrary hosts. Behavioral detection looks for that deviation from normal behavior.

Detection in Singularity AI SIEM

Platform detection content looks at what happens on the host after exploitation, not at the request body.

Attacker Step

Telemetry

Visible Indicators

Code execution in the service

Process creation

Shell processes whose lineage or prior image is node, nodejs, or bun, including an in-place exec, followed by enumeration utilities (id, whoami, uname, hostname) or sensitive file reads

Tooling download

Process creation, File creation

Downloaders (curl, wget, interpreters) fetching to world-writable paths, and executables written and then run from /tmp

Files written by the service

File creation

A Node.js service account writing new executables or scripts outside its normal application paths

Shell and C2

Process creation, IP Connect

Shell processes with a socket as standard input or output, socket-redirection patterns (/dev/tcp, nc, socat), and unexpected outbound connections from Node.js service accounts

Novel child process

First-seen analytics

A Node.js process that starts or becomes a shell or image it has never run in that environment

Correlation rules tie these together. A request to the service, or an outbound fetch to an untrusted host, followed by a process spawn or file drop from the same Node.js process is the shape of a successful chain.

Visibility at the Edge

Sysdig reports that the crash is easy to reproduce, which makes repeated worker crashes and restarts a useful early signal. Web server, WAF, and CDN logs may show requests with Content-Encoding: br followed by bursts of HTTP 5xx responses and unexplained worker restarts. Singularity AI SIEM can ingest those sources alongside endpoint data if you forward them.

Hunt with Purple AI While You Patch

Patching is the only complete fix. While that work runs, analysts can ask Purple AI questions such as:

Show me shell processes whose parent or prior image was node, nodejs, or bun since October 21.

Show me new executable files written by the Node.js service account since October 21.

Show me outbound connections from the Node.js service account to destinations we have never seen.

Show me hosts with a spike in 500 responses followed by a Node.js process restart.

The last question depends on web server logs being ingested.

Confirm Agent Saturation on Node.js Hosts

Confirm the agent is deployed, healthy, and in protect mode on every server and container host that runs Node.js, Bun, or another service that decompresses Brotli. Start with internet-facing Express 5 services and services that fetch external URLs.

Recipients should not rely solely on this report for security decisions and should consult with their security teams and SentinelOne account representatives for current guidance.

articles.context: He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security
articles.full_text:
In his LABScon 26 keynote, delivered in his inimitable comedic style, Harvard University professor James Mickens questions whether the scale of current AI investment is justified. Starting from US tech capex of roughly 1.4% of GDP in the second quarter of 2025, he argues that computers are already good enough, and notes that the world has so many CPUs and GPUs that they are put to work solving cryptocurrency puzzles to make imaginary money. More seriously, the AI models that investment is building, he says, grow increasingly opaque as their parameter counts rise.

Mickens then cites research and incident reports on model behaviour, including models acting to prevent another model being shut down and recent sandbox escapes at OpenAI and other labs. On economics, he rejects the assumptions that AI will create more jobs than it destroys and that universal basic income will follow widespread automation.

He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security. Mickens own contribution is Guillotine, a hypervisor design that runs a model’s CPU code on isolated cores unable to read or write the hardware state of the cores running the hypervisor. Arguing that hardware-based mechanisms for isolating misaligned frontier models will be an important direction for research over the next five years, he invites those interested in this approach to collaborate.

This keynote speaks to security practitioners and researchers interested in AI risk, the economics behind current AI investment, or hardware-level containment of frontier models

About the Author

James Mickens is a Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science at Harvard University. His research focuses on the performance, security, and privacy of large-scale online services; a current focus is the interpretability and sandboxing of potentially misaligned frontier models. Prior to becoming a professor at Harvard, Dr. Mickens spent seven years at Microsoft Research, working in the Distributed Systems group.

About LABScon

This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS.
